title: No. 5 Penn State women's hockey shuts out Lindenwood, earns series victory
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions complete the series sweep in front of a parent-filled crowd.

Following a thrilling 5-4 win in their first game of the series, No. 5 Penn State dominated with a 3-0 victory win its third straight match, the team's longest win streak of the season.

First Period

Penn State held the majority of possession for the first four minutes of the opening period, sending two shots on goal early.

Both Abby Stonehouse and Maddalena Bedont were then sent to the penalty box for holding, leading to a four-on-four power play. The Nittany Lions notched three shots before both teams returned to full strength.

The blue and white were aggressive offensively to start the game, holding a 10-2 total shots advantage within the first 10 minutes of play, and keeping Lindenwood’s goaltender active during that stretch.

The Penn State defense was also playing its part as well, holding the Lions to only two shots in 14 minutes of action. The blue and white stifled any breakaway opportunities and rarely allowed the puck to stay in its defensive zone for long periods of time.

As the game continued, the Nittany Lions kept inching closer to a goal, as Kylie Amelcovich missed a shot in front of the goal.

Penn State sophomore defender Danica Maynard asserted her dominance by scoring a goal after fighting for the puck in a scrum in front of the crease with under two minutes to go. Penn State exited the first period with a 1-0 lead.

Second Period

The momentum continued swinging in favor of the Nittany Lions. More sustained offensive attacks led to more opportunities to score, and the blue and white were crashing rebounds off of Lindenwood’s goaltender.

The Lions began to create chances of their own, possibly taking note of Penn State's attack. A couple moments where Morgan Stickney couldn’t secure the puck in the crease led to battles for the puck in front of the net. Yet, Stickney stood tall between the pipes.

Following a hooking call on Elina Zillox, the Nittany Lions earned their first power play of the match. Penn State continued to struggle finishing shots, as none of their six shots got past Lindenwood’s goaltender.

With nine minutes remaining in the second period, the blue and white had sent 40 shots compared to the Lions’ eight. They added five more in their second power play opportunity after Tatiana Blichova was called for roughing.

The Lions’ defense had made its best effort to bend but not break, and much of that could be attributed to Ebba Ridderstolpe’s performance. She had allowed just one goal while making 47 saves through two periods.

“I give that kid a lot of credit, like, I'm proud of her,” Jeff Kampersal said about the Lindenwood net minder. “She showed up today and she was stellar.”

Although the Nittany Lions couldn’t convert any of their chances, they dominated the half to retain a 1-0 lead.

Third Period

Within the first 20 seconds of the match, a scuffle near the Nittany Lions led to a coach's challenge by Jeff Kampersal. The referees determined that no foul occurred on the play.

“We saw the kid wind up from the bench, but it wasn’t like that on the video,” Kampersal said. “It didn’t look that bad.”

A penalty on Megan Hosman for body checking led to a power play for Lindenwood. The penalty kill unit finished unscathed.

Multiple chances to score were left on the ice, as Riddlestorpe continued to make clutch saves for the Lions. Another Lions player, Paige Cline, was called for holding, leading to a power play for Penn State. Amelcovich received a holding penalty of her own during the two minutes, as a Lindenwood power play ensued.

“It is frustrating to throw up 60 (shots) and only really have like two goals,” Kapersal said. “So we need to figure that part out, whether we need to be stronger around the net.”

However, the Lions’ woman-up advantage didn’t stop Penn State’s attack. A shorthanded goal scored by junior captain Grace Outwater added to the blue and white lead, taking a 2-0 advantage.

“I think it was a great PK by us, we changed it to a more aggressive style, and I think that really kind of scared them,” Outwater said.

Grace Tullock added to the Nittany Lions penalty count after being called for interference, granting Lindenwood another power play opportunity. Stickney made a key one-on-one save to hold the shutout, but another penalty for high-sticking on Morgan Walsh followed.

Penalties kept stacking on each other, as Michaela Paulinyova received an interference penalty, leading to four-on-four play until Penn State returned to full strength, where they’d have one minute of a woman-up advantage.

The blue and white nearly converted, but a referee whistled for a stoppage seconds before the puck saw the back of the net. The Nittany Lions left the power play empty handed.

As time was expiring, Lindenwood coach Max Gavin opted to play with six skaters on the ice. After a Penn State defensive stand led to a breakaway, Sofia Ismael lifted the puck over a defender and scored an open net goal to extend the lead to three goals with two minutes left.

The goal sealed the win for the Nittany Lions, as they completed the sweep with a 3-0 win over the Lindenwood Lions.

title: No. 15 Penn State women’s volleyball falls to UCLA in five sets to open California trip, falls in Big Ten standings
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State hit the sky to the Golden Coast, with a chance to snag a top-five spot in the Big Ten standings on the line.

The Nittany Lions ultimately started slow, a commonality this season, and despite an offensive flair, they fell 3-2 in a complete team performance over a UCLA squad that received votes in the recent AVCA poll,

Things between the blue and white and the blue and gold have always been tense, as the last two matches were split over five-set thrillers.

When things moved to the West Coast, the Bruins set the tone with a pair of kills, but the two squads stalled as they split the first 20 points of the opening set. UCLA then found a stride of form, flying to a 20-14 advantage via seven kills and the first ace of the match.

With coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley’s unit on the brink of surrender, Penn State regrouped on the sideline with a timeout, but it couldn’t stop UCLA from claiming the first set 25-20. The Bruins couldn’t run away with it, largely because right-side hitter Kennedys Martin logged four kills after the timeout.

Penn State came out of the gates with a burst in the second set, holding an 8-2 advantage, before outside 1hitter Whitney Lauenstein added the first Penn State ace of the match. This barrage couldn’t stop UCLA behind its raucous crowd.

The Bruins quickly caught up behind an efficient offense and a plethora of Penn State errors to set the frame at 15-11 going into the media timeout.

After the break, middle blocker Gabrielle Nichols recorded a block assist for her fourth total block of the match to that point, followed by an error and a Lauenstein kill to force another break — this time via a UCLA timeout.

To that point in the match, the dynamic duo of Lauenstein and Martin logged 21 of 28 total kills for Penn State.

Both teams started extremely efficiently after the breaks, with seven successful attacking attempts broken down into five kills and two aces split between the two squads, with Alexis Stucky smashing Penn State’s score from the backline.

Unfortunately for UCLA, the Nittany Lions’ depth prevailed in that stretch, as Nichols, Lauenstein, Martin and Falduto logged kills to push it to 23-14. Lauenstein committed an error to break the clean stretch, but it didn’t snap the trend, as Nichols and outside hitter Emmi Sellman knocked the decisive kills to tie the match at 1-1.

The blue and white’s offense started the third set 5-2, catalyzed by a Falduto ace. That flame faded, and Penn State got entangled in a slow dance with UCLA throughout the set, trading points up to a 16-15 advantage.

With a pair of Bruins’ errors, Martin did too, logging a kill and ace to push Penn State to 21-16 and force UCLA into its second timeout of the set.

The break was moot, as kills from middle blocker Kendall Northern and Lauenstein pushed Penn State to the finish line, while Sellman’s ace logged the decisive point to close out the third frame.

With seven clean kills and no errors to open the fourth set, Penn State’s offense led the show, with five. The Bruins kept the fight alive, cutting the deficit to 6-5, but Sellman stopped it in its tracks with two kills and an ace in a run that pushed the Nittany Lions to a 14-9 lead.

Penn State roared to a 17-10 advantage, but UCLA punched back with two kills, an error and an ace, ending any chance of early celebrations. That signaled what would be to come, as the Bruins battled back to a 22-22 set with an ace along the way.

Both squads fired off challenges to seize needed points, yet only UCLA’s was successful, which also pushed it to set point. The Bruins soon claimed the point to push it to a fifth set with a kill, as the Nittany Lions dropped a set in which they once held a seven-point advantage.

Sellman and Martin slammed kills in a 4-1 Penn State start, but they weren’t able to pull away from a UCLA unit that caught up quickly. However, the same blue and white duo that started the set hot continued their run with another set of kills to help the Nittany Lions pull away.

At 8-5, the Bruins called a timeout to stop the momentum, which sparked a small run to tie it up, but Penn State responded with one of its own: an ace from Lexi Gin. That led to another UCLA timeout, which sparked a four-point run to flip it for a 12-11 Bruins’ lead and caused a Penn State break.

That timeout paid little to no dividends, as UCLA knocked a crucial ace immediately after, and soon picked up the decisive kill to win 15-12.

In the win, Martin logged a season-high 25 kills, followed by Lauenstein’s 19, also a season-high. Sellman trailed the pair with nine kills but led Penn State with two aces. Nichols led at the net with nine total blocks and the only solo block for her squad, along with five kills.

With the result, the blue and white fall to 12-5 and 4-3 in conference play, losing a four-match win streak.

Up next

Penn State continues the California circuit tomorrow with a Saturday night clash against USC, set to start at 7 p.m.

title: Penn State men’s soccer rallies to draw in foul-heavy match against Northwestern
author: Darius Harandi | For the Collegian
description:
After a hard-fought scoreless draw at Michigan that secured Penn State’s first Big Ten point and snapped its five-game Big Ten losing streak, the Nittany Lions traveled in Evanston, Illinois, for Northwestern’s Alumni and Senior Night.

Both teams finished with 10 men, as neither side found a winner in the dying minutes, settling for a 1-1 draw.

Northwestern was looking to end its current slump, after being outscored 6-1 in its last two games, hoping to pick back up the form that resulted in a 4-0 win over then No. 2 Maryland. Penn State, meanwhile, had a chance to build momentum off its best conference result of the season.

First half

The first real threat came in the third minute, when strong hold-up play from the Wildcats led to a dangerous through ball. The play was intercepted at the last moment by Penn State defender Arian Recinos.

In the third minute, a cleared Northwestern corner kick led to a one-on-one counterattack, forcing Wildcats defender Fritz Volmar to pull down the sprinting Nittany Lions forward Etienne Reck. The foul initially drew a yellow card, which after review was later upgraded to a red.

Despite being a man down, the Wildcats found their first real chance in the 23rd minute through captain and defender Bryant Mayer’s long throw-in, leading to a header that sailed ever so slightly too high.

The Wildcats used their first substitution to adjust after Volmar’s red card, bringing on midfielder Marco Silva for forward Aaron O’Reilly.

In the 42nd minute, Wildcats defender Andrew Johnson beat two blue and white defenders with a nutmeg to win a corner kick.

The game continued its slow pace, with neither team registering a shot on target for nearly the entire half, until a deep cross from defender Arian Recinos found midfielder Vladislav Cherny in the 44th minute. The Nittany Lions were unable to capitalize on the opportunity, as the shot was saved by a fully stretched Northwestern goalkeeper Dominic Pereira.

Second half

Northwestern came out of the break on the front foot, and just a minute into the half,

midfielder Gabriel Smyth got on the end of a long throw-in and smashed a tight-angled shot into the top left corner, giving the Wildcats a 1-0 lead.

A dangerous 3-on-2 counterattack for the Nittany Lions was ended in the 49th minute when Reck overhit his pass to a relatively wide-open defender, Morgan Marshall.

Down one goal, Penn State continued to ramp up the pressure, eventually leading to a close-range chance for forward Amadou Kone in the 72nd minute. Pereira blocked the shot, and the ensuing corner saw the ball scramble among a multitude of players before landing in front of Reck, whose header was saved and cleared, leaving the Nittany Lions with another missed opportunity.

A Wildcats clearance sparked a counterattack, forcing Penn State goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese to rush out to the halfway line and boot the ball across the field. Killing any chances of a second Northwestern goal.

Continuing to push for a goal, the blue and white finally found its equalizer in the 78th minute when defender and captain Joe Sheridan took advantage of the confusion over a possible handball, placing the ball into the bottom left corner, evading every defender’s outstretched foot. The leveler, Sheridan’s second of the season, evened the game at 1-1.

Tensions continued through to the 90th minute, when Sheridan was shown a red card after an apparent verbal exchange.

The Nittany Lions claimed their second straight conference draw, moving to 2-7-2 and 0-5-2 in the Big Ten.

Up next

Penn State returns to Jeffery Field at 7 p.m. Tuesday to host Rutgers in its fourth-to-last regular season game.

title: Penn State men’s hockey outgunned by No. 8 Quinnipiac, drops home opener
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
The last time Penn State took the ice in front of its home crowd, it walked off with a dominant 6-2 win in the first round of the Big Ten Tournament and a more-than-likely shot at the national title.

Yet after the Nittany Lions fell short of their NCAA Tournament goals and spent the offseason retooling, they returned to Pegula Ice Arena on Friday for their home opener.

The blue and white dropped its first game back in front of the Roar Zone, 6-3, to No. 8 Quinnipiac behind a number of penalties and six unanswered goals.

“Right now, that is a very poorly coached team,” head coach Guy Gadowsky said. “You get doubled up on power play opportunities, you give up breakaways, and you’re not going to win. There’s no chance you should win, and that’s on me.”

Penn State came out hot against the Bobcats, with sophomore forward Shea Van Olm leading the way.

Van Olm had two key chances early on, with the best one coming just 30 seconds in, missing by inches as it rolled behind goaltender Christian Kirsch before eventually getting batted out of danger.

It wasn’t long before the blue and white broke the ice, however.

About five minutes into play at Pegula Ice Arena, Nick Fascia sent a stretch pass to freshman forward Justin Larose, who was waiting unseen behind two Bobcat defenders. Larose received the pass on a breakaway and netted his second collegiate goal after beating Kirsch with a backhand shot off the crossbar.

Quinnipiac had a key chance to answer after defenseman Jackson Smith was called for cross-checking and sent to the box just over two minutes after the score.

The Nittany Lions stood tall behind netminder Josh Fleming, however, and the penalty was negated with about 30 seconds left after Quinnipiac’s Mason Marcellus was called for interference.

The power play was erased again, this time for the blue and white, when Larose laid a hit that was called for unsportsmanlike conduct.

Neither team could capitalize on the back-to-back penalties, but it wasn’t long before Penn State doubled its lead.

Freshman forward Kaden Pitre registered his first collegiate point when his slot pass found defender Mac Gadowsky, who fired a shot through to the back of the net. Mac Gadowsky’s score was his second of the season, already exceeding his one-goal tally from last year.

The blue and white began with a hot start in the period, but cooled off after three unanswered goals by Quinnipiac to erase its lead.

“First give or take 10 minutes was, I think, our best 10 minutes of hockey this year yet, but we have to find a way to keep that going,” captain Reese Laubach said. “We got to be able to keep the energy up…not just curl up in a ball and die when they score on us.”

The Bobcats’ first goal came on the power play, after defenseman Caeden Herrington was whistled for interference. A scrum in front of Fleming ended when sophomore Antonin Verreault corralled a loose puck and put Quinnipiac on the board.

Star forward Ethan Wyttenbach — last season’s NCAA points leader — added to Quinnipiac’s lead just over two minutes later after scoring on an odd-man rush.

After Penn State was called for its fourth penalty of the period, this time on Van Olm for tripping, Marcellus gave the Bobcats their first lead of the night and headed into the first intermission trailing by a goal.

The second period started less eventful, with both teams fighting for possession.

Penalties once again reared their head for the Nittany Lions, and Smith was called for his second cross-checking penalty of the night about five minutes in.

“We were not disciplined. We were not smart,” Gadowsky said. “The penalties we took were avoidable. I want to be dead clear about that.”

Quinnipiac continued to capitalize on the man-advantage, and senior forward Jack Stockfish sailed a one-timer past Fleming from the high slot to extend his team’s lead.

Shortly after the goal, sophomore forward Lev Katzin was tangled up with a Bobcat, and, to the outcry of the Roar Zone, no penalty was called. Penn State seemed to regain some of its early momentum and turned up the physicality.

When Quinnipiac’s Markus Vidicek was called for tripping, the blue and white looked primed to cut into its deficit. Nothing came of the man-advantage, however, and the remaining minutes of the second period ticked down with few opportunities for Penn State.

With just 14 seconds left, Vidicek snuck a goal backdoor behind Fleming, sending the Nittany Lions into the final 20 minutes chasing a three-goal deficit.

The third period brought with it the blue and white’s penalty struggles, and a bench minor for too many men on the ice turned into Quinnipiac’s sixth straight unanswered goal.

Although much quieter than earlier in the night, sophomore forward Luke Misa breathed some life back into the building, collecting his own rebound off of Kirsch and cutting into the Bobcats’ lead with just over seven minutes to play.

Despite the late momentum surge, Misa’s goal proved to be the lone score for Penn State in the final period, dropping its home opener to No. 8 Quinnipiac, 6-3.

title: Penn State field hockey outlasts Ohio State in shootout victory
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
With less than 10 minutes to play on Friday night, it looked as if Penn State’s winning streak would extend to six games. Then, it seemed like Ohio State was on the brink of completing a two-goal late-game comeback to end it.

The blue and white ultimately won the coin flip, earning a shutout victory behind a complete team performance.

A last-second goal by Olivia Marthins sent the teams into overtime and gave each a clean slate.

Lara Pyle worked down the left wing on Penn State’s opening possession and fired the game’s opening shot on net, but Ohio State goaltender Maddie Stevens deflected it wide and out of danger.

Neither team could find a serious scoring chance in the first quarter’s opening stages. With about seven minutes to go in the frame, Marthins found herself in close on the Buckeye goal and fired a close-range shot that Stevens dropped low to reject.

Victoria Kutz sent a long pass into Ohio State’s offensive zone, and the ball bounced from stick to stick before the Nittany Lions cleared it. Soon after, Pyle worked free again and wound up for a backhand shot, but whiffed and fell face-first to the playing surface.

Penn State maintained offensive pressure despite failing to generate a second shot on goal in the first quarter. The frame ended in a scoreless deadlock.

Stevens made a quick save to open the second quarter before a Buckeye infraction gave Penn State its first penalty corner. Pyle received the pass and fired a shot that deflected off the post and out of play.

Ella Gaitan found a cutting Marthins, who flicked a backhand shot that Stevens deflected. Pyle jumped on the rebound and capitalized, burying it in the net for her first goal of the season.

Ohio State earned a penalty corner moments later, and equalized after Aby Deverka’s save rebounded to Autum Kernechel for a goal that closely mirrored Pyle’s preceding score.

After a flurry of offensive action at the start of the quarter, the units settled down as time drained off the second-frame clock. With just over two minutes until halftime, the Buckeyes got another penalty corner after a foul in the shooting circle couldn’t find the nylon.

To begin the second half, Penn State was awarded its second penalty corner. Gaitan fired from the edge of the circle, but the ball ricocheted off the post and into Ohio State’s possession.

The Buckeyes earned a corner in response, but couldn’t answer. The Nittany Lions defended Ohio State’s first shot and neutralized a second corner afterward.

Marthins intercepted a Buckeye pass and powered upfield. The ball found its way to Sienna Dunn, then back to Marthins, who smacked it past Stevens’ far side to put Penn State back in front with five minutes remaining in the third quarter.

Penn State began the fourth frame with an advantage after Carmela Maro was shown a green card, but couldn’t capitalize. With just under nine minutes to play, Ohio State had a strong scoring chance that looked like a save by Deverka until the referee called for a penalty corner.

A review upheld the call and Deverka made her sixth save to maintain the Nittany Lions’ lead. Seconds later, Sienna Golden beat her with a tip-in to level the game in its closing stages.

Golden nearly gave Ohio State the lead just moments later on a shot that sailed just wide of the post. The Buckeyes dominated offensively, and Deverka made a big save before they earned yet another penalty corner.

A low, driven shot from Phillippa Jowett beat Deverka on her right side and put Ohio State up by one with five minutes left on the clock.

Penn State earned a penalty corner with less than three minutes to play, but Stevens bailed out the Buckeyes with a diving save that held their lead. With 20 ticks on the clock, the referees went to a review and awarded a Nittany Lion penalty corner.

After Stevens made an initial save, Marthins tucked the rebound into the nylon to send the contest to overtime.

She drove into the circle at the start of the extra period before being stripped of the ball to end the scoring chance. Ohio State pushed into the offensive zone and threatened Deverka, and the Buckeyes won a penalty corner to create their best chance of overtime so far.

The Buckeye shot deflected around the zone and away from the net before Ohio State earned a second consecutive corner, one that was also fruitless. Soon after, the third Buckeye penalty corner in quick succession proved to be no help, as it was saved as well.

On the other end, Marthins drove into the shooting circle and won Penn State a corner of its own. Stevens continued to hold strong and keep the game alive with a high-level save. An intercepted Buckeye pass led to Penn State’s sixth corner, but a bad pass trickled out of the circle and into its defensive half.

Neither squad could find the net in 15 overtime minutes, so they took to a shootout to settle things.

Ella Gaitan was up first for Penn State, and she faked to the backhand before tucking a wraparound shot into the net. Deverka saved the first shot she faced, and Dunn found the net to give Penn State an advantage.

Katie Fichtner scored for Ohio State, and Stevens made her first save of the shootout before making another on Natalie Freeman.

Kernechel missed her shot, and a review kept Marthins from putting her third ball of the evening into the net. Emily Barker sailed her shot wide left before Pyle deked to the right and sunk her shot to clinch the win for Penn State.

Up next

Penn State will host Michigan on Sunday, with faceoff set for noon.

title: No. 5 Penn State women's hockey earns win over Lindenwood in high-scoring barnburner
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Family Weekend began on the ice on a rainy day in Happy Valley.

Penn State capitalized on its home-turf advantage at Pegula Ice Arena, earning a 5-4 win over AHA foe Lindenwood in a game where the goals trickled like raindrops for a full 60 minutes.

The blue and white entered the contest after dropping only one game in conference play in the early weeks, setting up a series sweep opportunity tomorrow.

First period

The first period started pretty even, with both teams getting quality shots on goal. Penn State controlled the puck for most of the period, while Lindenwood prioritized the odd-man breakaway counterattack. The Nittany Lions ran into trouble at 8:48 when Lindenwood earned a power play after a body-checking penalty on McKenna Walsh.

The penalty kill proved stout and subdued Lindenwood’s power-play unit. Immediately after returning to full strength, the blue and white hit paydirt after Walsh left the box and scored a breakaway 2-on-1 goal assisted by Sophie Morrow to put the Nittany Lions ahead 1-0. The rest of the period was back-and-forth, with Penn State and Lindenwood trading shots.

Forward Sofia Ismael continued to stand out early in the game. Every time the puck was on the freshman’s stick, she made a dazzling move to either pass to a teammate or get a shot off. Nonetheless, the Period ended 1-0 Nittany Lions.

Second period

Lindenwood started the second period hot, scoring 46 seconds in when Paige Cline tied to at 1-1. Morrow blundered by losing the puck in front of the net, allowing Lindenwood’s Raquel McCormack to assist Cline.

Minutes later, Penn State earned a power play after a hooking call on Michaela Paulinyova, and the Nittany Lions took virtually no time to score after Morrow’s long-range shot was deflected off Lindenwood Netminder Ebba Ridderstople onto Kylie Amelkovich’s stick to make it 2-1 Penn State.

The blue and white then found themselves in penalty trouble when Alanna Devlin received a hooking penalty, which allowed Lindenwood to knot up the game 2-2 after a beautiful one-time slap shot by left wing Silje Gundersen.

The Lions then continued the momentum, scoring a minute later after a top-right screamer by Krisztina Weiler, assisted by Cline, making the score 3-2 Lindenwood at 8:46 minutes into the second period.

The second-half scoring barrage continued four minutes later after Penn State's Amelkovich got her second goal of the game after a long-range shot by Grace Tullock was deflected off of Ridderstolpe onto her stick. The high-scoring period ended with the game knotted at 3-3.

Third period

The third period started with a barrage of shots by the Nittany Lions that nearly led to a goal after Devlin’s shot hit the left post.

Penn State seemed to play fast and attack with lots of urgency, as multiple lines continued to get shots off.

The good play by the lie down white paid off after a great sequence of attacking play. Grace Outwater flew on a breakaway; the goaltender deflected her shot onto Minkah Keller’s stick, who passed it to Hall in front of the net, and to her right was Outwater, who slotted it in to give Penn State a 4-3 lead with 12:07 left in the third period.

Lindenwood did not lie down after that, though; with 8:57 left on the clock, the Lions got a breakaway 2-on-1 where McCormack assisted Cline for her second goal of the game, tying the score at 4-3.

The Nittany Lions found the game-winning goal with 5:22 left in the period after a stroke of brilliance by Morrow, who danced up the left side of the ice and beat the netminder with a shot to the right.

Penn State's defense then hunkered down for the next five minutes and closed the game with the win.

The Nittany Lions earned a gritty win, built on a response to adversity, to improve to 4-3 off back-to-back wins.

Having Grace Ouwater back from Canada’s training camp proved to be a real decider in this matchup alongside a two-goal performance by Amelkovich.

Up next

The series against Lindenwood concludes tomorrow at noon, giving the Nittany Lions another chance to stop Lindenwood’s seemingly explosive attack.

title: Registration, mail-in ballots | What students should know about voting ahead of midterm elections
author: Annabella Chaklos | The Daily Collegian
description:
As the midterm elections approach, many students may find themselves without a plan for the polls, especially if it’s their first time voting.

Election Day arrives on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Before it does, here’s a guide to understanding voter registration, mail-in ballots, identification requirements and in-person voting.

Voter registration

Before students can vote, they have to make sure they’re registered voters. Eligible students can register to vote at their local address on or off campus as long as they have lived there for 30 days, or they can register to vote at their hometown addresses, either in Pennsylvania or out-of-state.

The deadline to register in Pennsylvania is Oct. 19. Registration can be completed online. If an out-of-state student plans to vote in their home state, registration and voter information can be found at vote.gov.

Mail-in ballots

If a student is registered in their hometown or home state, they can request an absentee ballot to vote there by mail. The deadline to apply for a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania is Oct. 27, but deadlines for other states vary. Some states may also require voters to provide a reason for using an absentee ballot.

It’s suggested that voters request mail-in ballots as soon as possible so they can be filled out and returned by mail, a ballot drop box, the county election office or any other officially designated locations.Voters must return their own ballots unless they have a disability and have designated someone in writing to deliver their ballot for them using a Designated Agent Form, per Pennsylvania law.

Pennsylvania mail-in ballots should be filled out in blue or black ink and sealed in the yellow envelope marked "official election ballot.” The yellow envelope should be enclosed in the pre-addressed outer return envelope, and voters must sign the voter’s declaration on the outside of the outer return envelope, with the current date written on it.

Voters registered in Centre County can use local drop boxes, like the one outside the HUB-Robeson Center or at the State College Municipal Building, 243 S Allen St. Voters registered in other counties or states must return their ballots by mail.

Mail-in ballots must be returned to its rightful county by 8 p.m on Election Day, which is Tuesday, Nov. 3 to be counted.

In-person voting

Voters planning to vote in person on Election Day should know their designated polling place, which is based on the address they registered, and can be found here. Pennsylvania polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., but if a voter enters the line at the polls by 8 p.m., they’ll still be able to vote.

At the polls, voters should be prepared to wait in line, especially if voting in the mornings or evenings, which are the busiest times. From there, they’ll check in with a poll worker, mark either a paper or a digital ballot and cast their vote.

Voter identification

At the polls, first-time voters must bring a form of photo or non-photo identification. Returning voters do not need to show a form of identification unless they have changed polling locations.

Acceptable forms of photo identifications as long as they are not expired, revoked or canceled are:

A Pennsylvania driver’s licensePennDOT ID cardID issued by any commonwealth agencyID issued by the U.S. governmentU.S. passportU.S. Armed Forces IDStudent ID (including an electronic/digital student ID card)Employee ID.

Non-photo forms of identification are permitted as long as they show a valid name and address, and can include a confirmation issued by the county voter registration office, such as:

A voter registration cardNon-photo ID issued by the commonwealthNon-photo ID issued by the U.S. governmentFirearm permitCurrent utility billCurrent bank statementPaycheckGovernment check

title: No. 5 Penn State women's hockey to host Lindenwood for Family Weekend
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State takes on Lindenwood in a two-game set Friday and Saturday in Pegula Ice Arena.

The Nittany Lions are coming off a split series against Syracuse, losing 5-4 in overtime then winning 4-0 the next day. The series resulted in a ranking drop, putting the Nittany Lions at No. 5 in the country after entering the season one spot higher. The blue and white hope to put the upset loss behind them and get back on track this weekend.

The Lions are 4-4 after two losses to AHA opponent Mercyhurst; they are 1-3 in conference play. Scoring is evenly spread for Lindenwood, with 14 players having two points or more. Junior defenseman Elina Zilliox and true freshman forward Tilde Simensen share the lead in points, each with six points so far this season. Forwards Paige Cline and Tatiana Blichova share the scoring title for the Lions, with three goals each.

When asked about Lindenwood, Jeff Kampersal acknowledged they look good and could cause some issues.

“You look at their program, and it looks like they're having fun; obviously, they've enjoyed a little success so far this season,” Kampersal said. “On tape, they look quick, and they look like they're moving the puck well. Like all the AHA teams we play, we don't want to take penalties and give them power-play opportunities because that's more likely when they will strike.”

In between the pipes for both units, there’s been heavy rotation. For Lindenwood, it’s used three netminders: Ebba Ridderstolpe, Madison Bowtell and Eva Filippova. Ridderstolpe and Bowtell saw most of the action, splitting seven of eight starts and both posting a goals-against average under two and save percentages north of .940.

For Penn State it’s been Maddy Campbell and Morgan Stickney splitting action in the crease, as sophomore goaltender Campbell has been the leading act. The Courtice, Ontario, native has appeared in four of the Nittany Lions’ six games, with a .944 save percentage and a 1.23 goals-against average.

Syracuse's speed and counterattack did prove to give the Nittany Lions a little trouble last series, so Kampersall and his team will have a chance to bounce back in possession and not give Lindenwood odd numbers on the counterattack.

“So we need to essentially lock it down from the beginning defensively so we can play a good offense and prevent them from having the puck too much,” Kampersal said. “But (Lindenwood) presents issues like Syracuse did with their speed.”

Last week, the blue and white were missing two key contributors, Grace Outwater and Abby Stonehouse, who were participating in Canada’s National Women's team training camp in Quebec, Canada, which wraps up on Thursday.

It adds to a laundry list of unavailable skaters in the offensive front, as forward Matilde Fantin is also sidelined with an injury. With Outwater and Stonehouse potentially being unavailable this series as well, the Nittany Lions need to lean on depth scorers like Kylie Amelkovich, Sofia Ismael and Nicole Hall to keep producing goals at a high level if they want a series win this weekend.

title: Penn State vs. Michigan preview | Forecast, broadcast info ahead of Big House matchup
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State and Michigan will meet at 3:30 p.m. Saturday to decide who earns its first Big Ten win of the season.

The Wolverines hold the all-time series advantage, 17-10, and are currently on a three-game win streak dating back to 2021. However, both programs feature first-year head coaches who came from Big 12 schools in Kyle Whittingham (Utah) and Matt Campbell (Iowa State).

Here’s the forecast, betting odds, broadcasting information and additional team details to know heading into Penn State’s Week 7 action.

Forecast

The Big House will experience true, crisp October weather for the Saturday ball game.

There’ll be intermittent clouds that gradually eclipse the sun throughout the game, according to AccuWeather.

The temperature will be 59 degrees at kickoff and remain mostly steady throughout the contest, reaching a low of 56 with a real feel of 50 due to a 66% chance of rain in the second half.

Betting, how to watch

Both Penn State and Michigan are winless in the Big Ten, but the Wolverines are 6.5-point favorites on their home turf, according to FanDuel.

With an over/under set at 42.5 points, the sportsbooks expect a 24-17 Michigan victory.

The game will be broadcast on CBS and streamed live on Paramount+. Tickets are available for as low as $39 on Ticketmaster.

About Michigan

Coming off a bye, the Wolverines are seeking their first conference win of the season. Michigan fell to then-No. 17 Iowa, 20-19, and unranked Minnesota, 20-16.

Michigan’s season kicked off in controversy when the Wolverines’ 13-12 victory over Western Michigan in Week 1 was decided by a hail mary throw with one second on the clock. That one second was added after the video review, and the Division I FBS Oversight Committee released a statement saying proper protocol wasn't followed in the review.

As for the players, sophomore quarterback Bryce Underwood’s inconsistency in the pass game is juxtaposed by his mobility. He currently has a 59.29% completion rate with 881 passing yards, five touchdowns and four interceptions while rushing for a team-high 256 yards and two touchdowns.

Underwood returns to Ann Arbor after his worst performance of the season when he went 10-for-21 for 101 yards and two interceptions in the loss to the Golden Gophers.

Wide receiver JJ Buchanan leads the Wolverines with 446 receiving yards and four touchdowns, followed by wide receiver Andrew Marsh who has 268 yards and a touchdown.

Michigan added two midseason transfers ahead of the game — former Miami tight end Alex Bauman and former Boise State cornerback Jeremiah Earby — after being granted another year of eligibility.

Bauman had 166 receiving yards on 18 catches as a Hurricane while Earby was named second-time All-Mountain West after making 60 tackles and four interceptions. They likely won’t make an impact this week as they adjust to learning the Wolverines’ playbooks.

About Penn State

Penn State’s offense got into a better rhythm despite losing to USC, 31-23, in the White Out game last week. Rocco Becht threw for 289 yards and a touchdown, bouncing back from an inconsistent performance against Northwestern.

The defensive secondary was torched by Jayden Maiava’s passing attack. It was an uncharacteristic performance by the unit overall, which allowed 301 passing yards and three touchdowns.

The Nittany Lions’ run game, once again, couldn’t generate meaningful offense against the USC. Penn State only played running backs Carson Hansen and James Peoples, who combined for 48 yards on 21 carries.

Penn State did, however, find its identity as a pass-first team, and Becht’s 1,397 passing yards and 11 touchdowns show it. With wide receiver Koby Howard still out due to injury, Becht has relied heavily on wide receiver Chase Sowell for offensive production.

Sowell currently has 359 receiving yards and two touchdowns. Meanwhile, tight end Benjamin Brahmer has a team-high three receiving touchdowns, but hasn’t been utilized in the passing game as much as Taylor Mouser would like.

“I need to make sure that we get him the ball more because he is one of our best players, and that's a focal point for me every week, and has been for the last couple years,” Mouser said Tuesday.

Tony Rojas continues to be Penn State’s ace on defense, leading the Nittany Lions with 44 tackles, 8.5 tackles for loss, four sacks, two interceptions, two pass breakups, two quarterback hurries and a forced fumble.

Outside of Rojas, Penn State’s pass rush has been an issue all season long, with Yvan Kemajou and Caleb Bacon being the only edge rushers with a sack. Linebacker Alex Tatsch has the only other sack on the team, but he was ruled out with a season-ending injury.

title: Players to watch | QB Bryce Underwood, DE John Henry Daley highlight Michigan’s top talent
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Amidst a three-game losing streak, Penn State will travel to Ann Arbor to face Michigan at 3:30 p.m. Saturday.

The Wolverines had high expectations coming into the year, but a last-second victory over Western Michigan in the season opener and back-to-back losses to No. 17 Iowa and Minnesota have pushed them out of the AP Poll and into the middle of the Big Ten.

Despite the struggles, Michigan is home to many elite players, including the No. 1 recruit in the Class of 2025.

JJ Buchanan, wide receiver

The Big Ten is full of star-studded wide receivers, and JJ Buchanan tops the list for Michigan. Through five games, he leads the team with 446 yards and four touchdowns, averaging 18.6 yards per catch.

Buchanan’s height gives him a major advantage downfield, as he stands at 6-foot-4. That may come as an issue Saturday, as Penn State’s tallest cornerback who plays regularly is 6-foot-2 Josiah Zayas.

The Wolverines have faced top-25 opponents twice this season, and after Buchanan’s contribution against then-No. 11 Oklahoma was limited, he was a key factor against No. 17 Iowa. He recorded five receptions for 130 yards and two touchdowns.

Even in his down weeks, Buchanan has been a consistent target for Underwood. He’s recorded multiple catches in all five games and has tallied more than 50 yards in all but one contest.

John Henry Daley, defensive end

While he hasn’t performed to the level he did at Utah last year, John Henry Daley was a crucial player for Kyle Whittingham to bring to Ann Arbor.

Daley recorded 11.5 sacks and two forced fumbles for the Utes in 2025 and already has three sacks this year. However, he left the field mid game on Sept. 26 against Iowa with a left ankle injury — the same ankle in which he ruptured his achilles in November — and was out against Minnesota and is questionable as of Wednesday’s availability report.

Daley tallied 1.5 sacks against Oklahoma quarterback John Mateer, adding eight tackles in the team’s win.

Bryce Underwood, quarterback

Underwood came to Michigan as the top-rated athlete in his class, earning an NIL package valued nearly $12 million. Despite the money, he hasn’t lived up to the hype.

He started all 13 games as a true freshman in 2025, but threw an abysmal 11 touchdowns with nine interceptions and 60.3% accuracy. Underwood was also sacked 20 times.

Things haven’t been any better this year, as he’s only thrown five touchdowns with four interceptions.

However, he’s proven to be a threat with his legs. So far in 2026, Underwood has run for 212 yards and two touchdowns, including a career-long 38-yard rush.

Troy Bowles, linebacker

Linebacker Troy Bowles has been Michgian’s leading tackler through five games, recording 40 total tackles. He’s also the son of Tampa Bay Buccaneer’s head coach Todd Bowles, who’s known for his defensive scheming.

Bowles has been a key figure in the Wolverine’s run defense, which has the potential to shine against Penn State’s unestablished running game. He has 4.5 tackles for loss and a pair of quarterback hits.

However, one of Bowles’ most notable moments from this season was his fumble recovery against Oklahoma, where he forced Mateer and the Sooners to stall out amid a long drive.

title: Column | Expectations for Penn State women’s soccer in remainder of 2026 campaign
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
With just four regular-season games remaining in the 2026 season, Penn State has showcased its skills and teamwork capabilities on the pitch, giving fans a little taste of what is to come in the remainder of the year.

The Nittany Lions are 6-3-4 on the season and 4-2-2 in Big Ten play. The blue and white is unbeaten at Jeffrey Field, holding a record of 4-0-3, but struggle on the road, where it sits at 2-3-1.

Penn State’s previous matches offer plenty to unpack, but here is what to expect going forward.

Top performers

Penn State has a diverse lineup of talent, but there are three leading players on its roster this season and it’s no shock who is headlining the group.

Aubrey Kulpa has been outstanding for the blue and white this year. The junior forward has recorded 15 points via six goals and three assists while also tallying 39 shots.

The Cromwell, Connecticut, native has been a force to be reckoned with all year, starting in every Penn State match and logging 990 minutes, the second most in the Nittany Lions’ lineup. Kulpa is expected to continue this momentum and be the player that future opponents Rutgers, No. 5 Michigan State, No. 25 Michigan and Indiana have to stop.

Kulpa’s production in the remaining regular season matches will be a huge factor in Penn State's postseason play, where she is expected to continue her leading offensive facilitation.

On the other end of the field, Kayleigh Herr has proven time and time again why she is the backbone of the Nittany Lions’ defense. The blue and white have totaled six shutout wins and have yet to concede more than two goals in a match.

The redshirt senior defender has the most minutes for Penn State at 1,147, showcasing how much coach Dambach relies on her to keep the back line intact.

The Cary, North Carolina, native’s aggression and composure are what make her a top performer for the Nittany Lions. Herr has been phenomenal for the program and will continue to be the defensive leader in the remainder of the season for the blue and white while competition levels only increase.

Staying on Penn State’s defensive end, Mackenzie Gress is a third standout player to recognize this season. The redshirt senior captain and starting goalkeeper has a save percentage of 0.818 on the season, playing in all but 32 minutes of total minutes possible.

The Lyndhurst, New Jersey, native was named Big Ten Goalkeeper of the Week on Sept. 1 after two clean sheets and followed up two days later, recording 10 saves against Virginia Tech, a career best.

Gress has yet to slow down and is expected to carry this momentum heading into the remainder of the regular season and tournament play.

Big Ten Tournament

Penn State has qualified for the Big Ten Tournament every season in program history, and fans don't expect anything different.

Last season, the Nittany Lions had a close call moment when it all came down to their performance against Ohio State on Oct. 25 for a win and in scenario. They ultimately defeated the Buckeyes 2-0.

The blue and white have a 41-16-6 overall record in the Big Ten Tournament. Penn State has tallied 25 wins on neutral sites and remains 12-3-0 at Jeffrey Field.

With a history of tournament dominance, Penn State is widely expected to reach at least the quarterfinals.

NCAA run

The Nittany Lions soccer program extended its 31st consecutive appearance in the NCAA Tournament last season. The blue and white hold the second-longest streak, behind North Carolina, which appeared in all 44.

This streak is rare in Division I soccer, as Penn State is joined by top programs North Carolina, Virginia, Santa Clara, Stanford, UConn, and Notre Dame, all of which have made 31+ appearances in the tournament.

Making the playoffs since 1995 sets a high bar for Penn State heading into the 2026 tournament, with expectations of either an automatic or at-large bid.

In the last postseason, the Nittany Lions easily swept Army 3-0 in the first round but fell to then-No. 1 Virginia in the second. This performance is expected to be matched, if not beaten in this year behind these three top names.

title: Setting the State College bar scene
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Being 21 in State College is, quite frankly, awesome. You unlock an adventurous checkpoint when you reach the golden age. You’re now free to roam Allen Street and College Avenue, along with the other congregating masses of students looking to blow off steam.

So, where do you go? How do you know what's popular? How will you know where the good deals are? Well, fortunately, on any given night of the week you can answer all three of those at the same time.

It's very simple: follow suit.

Wherever the deals are, the people go — wherever the most people go, that’s what's popular that night.

The State College bar scene is like its very own ecosystem. It feeds on one revolving, symbiotic cycle of various deals, settings and experiences.

For those that are already 21 or older, this guide will seem like a simple reminder. However, for those with birthdays on the near-horizon, this will serve as a bucket list, a set of ritual instructions, the one and only guide you’ll need. At least for the time being.

Now, say it’s the stroke of midnight and you’ve just turned 21. Where’s the first stop? Don’t worry, it won't be hard to find once you're downtown.

Phyrst

Located at 111 E. Beaver Ave, Phyrst has long been the starting point from which newly eligible State College drinkers begin their journey. After standing in line with the other patrons, you head down a staircase lined with framed photos of, literally, hundreds of people who got their picture taken on that same staircase for their 21st birthday.

Once you get your snapshot and step down into the packed and grungy basement, with the ceiling hanging low and the live band blasting through the cavernous walls, head straight for the bar. This is where the ritual begins. As is tradition at Phyrst, the first order is a classic and strangely named, “21st Blowjob Shot.”

A delectable and simplistic combination of Kahlua and Irish cream liqueur, topped with whipped cream, is as great an introduction to being 21 in State College as you can get. Since this is definitely the first time in your entire life that you’ve ever tasted alcohol, this is a perfect first order to make.

Champs Downtown

After that, it's open season. The streets are now mere headlights pointing you toward any opportunity of a grand ol’ time. Since you’ve got a taste for the energy that comes alive when bar doors are unlocked, you might want to head to what is considered the most popular bar spot: Champs Downtown.

If you're lucky enough to have your birthday fall on a Thursday, then both you and your wallet are in luck. Every Thursday at Champs, eager customers can purchase single-shot vodka sodas for one dollar each. Known as Dollar Vodka Soda Night (DVSN), Thursdays draw the biggest line of any bar on any day. People will wait for close to an hour just to take part in this college-oriented deal.

Want something a little sweeter than a watered down vodka soda? Try their “Dirty Sprite,” a less watered-down mixed drink with grape vodka, blue Curaçao liqueur, Sprite and a splash of cranberry juice for just two dollars.

Since Champs is normally mobbed with customers, and a trip to the bar for one more round normally turns into overcoming a human obstacle course, rigged with unpredictably jabbing pool cues and quicksand-like strips of spilled drinks, you might want to get some air.

Fret not — there’s a confident series of well-patronized bars that would love to see you sipping your drink and enjoying the company of close friends under the stars. Or, at least, dusty over hangs under the stars.

Some of State College's popular outdoor locations (if crowds permit) include Bill Pickle’s Tap Room, Cafe 210 West and Doggie’s Pub. While Pickle’s outdoor seating is small, it's sort of the “observation deck” for the Allen Street bar scene.

Sitting at a table on the small deck that peaks into the sidewalk, you're able to enjoy your drink and watch the seas of people passing from bar to bar, yelling for their friends to hurry up, slow down or stop for pizza.

If you want a little more room, but still a relaxed crowd, head a block down to W. College Avenue where you’ll find Cafe 210 West. The glowing green sign welcomes you into a large, outdoor patio. Sit around and watch the game on the projector screen hanging from the wall after you order your pitcher of whatever liquor they’re selling that night.

Doggie’s

After sitting and engaging in general sloth behavior, you might want to get the endorphins moving again. This is where Doggie’s Pub comes in as a saving grace.

The establishment, which was recently renovated, has one of the biggest outdoor areas of all the bars. With several large picnic tables, chairs, an outdoor bar and multiple cornhole sets, this bar has become a staple destination for many newly introduced customers.

With one of the largest menus in terms of deals, ranging from well cocktails, draft beers, canned cocktails and shots to discounts on housemade pizza, along with their pleasant outdoor lounge, Doggie’s is an essential landing spot for any time of night.

While there are other charming establishments in the State College bar scene, like Brothers Bar and Grill, Sharkies, Local Whiskey and The Shandygaff, these bars are each known for something specific, which is why they're so popular.

Each bar in State College sells a lot more than alcohol. There's something that defines them as a separate experience from the others. After all, they’re bars — they’re in the business of a good time, and State College customers are always in high demand.

author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian

title: Penn State LB Tony Rojas named to AP Midseason All-America team
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State's star defensive player has received midseason recognition.

Tony Rojas was named to the AP Midseason All-America second team.

Rojas has been the Nittany Lions' best defensive player through the first six weeks. He's Penn State's leading tackler with 43, which is 10 more than the next highest on the team.

title: Penn State CB Josiah Zayas, RB Carson Hansen off injury report ahead of Michigan
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Some significant developments have taken place on Penn State's availability report ahead of Saturday's game against Michigan.

Running back Carson Hansen and cornerback Josiah Zayas are off the report after being listed as probable Wednesday, while wide receiver Chase Sowell and linebacker Cam Smith are now listed as probable.

Smith was listed as questionable on Wednesday. His upgrade is good news for the Nittany Lions after Matt Campbell announced linebacker Alex Tatsch is out for the season on Wednesday.

title: Keep calm and wag on | Penn State’s CAPS hosts Caring Canines event
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Thursday, students had the opportunity to de-stress from midterm exams with Caring Canines, an event hosted by the Penn State Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) on the Student Health Center lawn. CAPS is the primary mental health provider for Penn State students at the University Park and Commonwealth campuses.

At the event, there was a variety of six dogs, each one varying in size, breed and, of course, fluffiness. They sat ready to soothe students, expectantly waiting to be given one of the many treats that were at the event for them. There were even some human treats — candy.

One of the fluffy, stress-relievers was Sully, a six-year-old border collie, who loves people. Sully’s owner, Sue Eshelman, 67, from Stormstown, Pennsylvania, said her daughter found him after her previous dog had passed away. She named him after the 2016 movie, “Sully,” and retired American aircraft pilot and diplomat, Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger.

“We do all kinds of dog sports with him,” Eshelman said. “We do a little agility with him, a little sheep herding with him.”

Every Thursday, Sully herds sheep, as his breed consists of world-renowned sheep herders. Eshelman said Sully enjoys meeting people the most, no matter their age.

“He just loves to go into nursing homes," Eshelman said. "He just sits by the wheelchair, and the people just pet him.”

Next, there was Micah, an eight-year-old Samoyed, who is a certified therapy dog, and has a lot of fluff to go around. Hellen Smith, Micah’s owner, from Pennsylvania Furnace, said she adopted Micah at 10-weeks-old, and he has been a certified therapy dog for two years.

Smith said Micah had to undergo surgery last May because he had an infection in part of his small intestine, but Micah has been much better since. During recovery, Micah’s owner said he did miss his job, but don’t worry, Micah got plenty of pets and cuddles from students to make up for it.

Smith explained that the majority of the owners at the event were retired, including herself, since therapy dogs are typically needed at sporadic times during the day, when most people are working.

Many students said the Caring Canines was a much needed break for them, especially during midterms season.

Brandon Ress, 19, of Boca Raton, Florida, said he first heard about the event hosted by CAPS from his resident assistant, who showed him the poster for it, but he wasn’t quite sure if he could make it or not.

Ress, a first-year studying journalism, said he was walking back to his dorm, coming from an exam, when he saw the dogs and realized it was the same event from the poster— he knew what he had to do.

Each dog had their own quirky and unique tricks that students were awed by.One dog in particular gathered a crowd from a special, and cute, trick of hers. April, a seven-year-old dachshund mix, loved the attention, or, rather, the treats she earned from her stand and begging, also called “sit pretty.”

“I love dogs, I mean, who doesn’t, but all the stress from my exam was washed away,” Ress said.

title: Penn State offense looking to get more receivers involved with WR Koby Howard’s return looming
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State tight end Benjamin Brahmer made his first reception of the Nittany Lions’ game against USC a few minutes into the fourth quarter.

The 4-yard catch would be Brahmer’s only of the game in Penn State’s 31-23 loss in the White Out.

“I told him after the game that for him to have one catch, it's unacceptable,” Taylor Mouser said Tuesday. “And on my sheet, my targets to get Ben the ball, we called all the plays that I had starred to get him the ball, and for whatever reason, they took it away.”

Brahmer was expected to see an increase in targets after wide receiver Koby Howard went down with an injury before Big Ten play, but both he and the tight ends as a whole haven’t seen much increase since Week 3.

Tight end Andrew Rappleyea did come down with seven receptions for 63 yards in Saturday’s contest. Tight end Gabe Burkle only has four total catches on the season, and he believes that getting as many receiving threats as possible into the game can only benefit Penn State.

“As much as we can kind of diversify who's getting the ball, I think that plays in our favor,” Burkle said.

Burkle mentioned the benefits of getting Brahmer, who was a John Mackey Award semifinalist in 2025, more involved.

“He's made some amazing plays already, and I think he's shown why it's so important to get him the ball,” Burkle said. “But getting him the ball just opens up so many other lanes for other people to get open in the passing game because they have to focus on him.”

Another player who could get more involved in the passing game is receiver Amarion Jackson. The true freshman earned a lot of praise prior to the season, especially after he made the full-time transition to wide receiver.

Without Howard, it’s been mainly wide receivers Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen involved, even though the Nittany Lions thrived offensively with three receivers on the field in the first three games.

“We gotta find a way to get (Jackson) involved a little bit more,” Mouser said. “He's earning the right to be able to do it, and in my eyes, he is trusted, and I certainly would expect to see him getting a lot more snaps the rest of the way here.”

Those snaps could take a decrease with Howard’s return on the horizon, however. His presence on the field has been missed by his teammates and coaches, as he was the Nittany Lions’ leading receiver prior to his injury against Buffalo.

“I think about Koby coming back a lot, so I'm very excited and I’m telling him that a lot, we certainly miss him just from the energy that he provides to the offense,” Mouser said.

Howard and the staff are looking at a “post-bye week conversation,” according to Matt Campbell, in terms of when he returns to game action.

It’s later than what Howard’s initial speculated return was, as he posted on his Instagram story with the date of Saturday’s matchup against Michigan when his injury first became public. Penn State will still be without Howard on Saturday as he’s already ruled out on the initial availability report.

“Koby is doing a really great job in terms of working his way back, and it's if anybody's going to get back sooner than later, it'll be Koby Howard just because of how he works,” Campbell said.

When he does make his return, he’s going to be expected to jump right back in and make an impact in the way he did before his injury. While that could be difficult, Mouser and Campbell have the belief he can do it given his work ethic.

Becht believes Howard’s return will free up the offense even more, and it could also mean some additional success in the run game with Penn State’s top weapon back on the field.

“Having that extra ability to have a weapon out there definitely frees us up a little bit, and definitely moves the defense off of us a little bit,” Becht said. “So we're able to do the run game still, and we're able to pass the ball down the field.”

title: Penn State men’s hockey set to host No. 8 Quinnipiac in home opener
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is coming home to Hockey Valley.

Penn State fell out of the USCHO poll after losing its first two games of the season. They were outscored 9-4 in the Ice Breaker Tournament against then-No. 16 UConn and Sacred Heart.

The blue and white are set to return to Happy Valley in hopes that a home opener can get the new-look team in the win column. However, a dominant No. 8 Quinnipiac has a chance to spoil it.

Scouting Quinnipiac

After Penn State faced growing pains in the season opener, the Nittany Lions will have to fix their mistakes quickly with a dominant offense coming into town. The Bobcats proved why they were ranked sixth in the preseason poll through their first four games.

Ethan Wyttenbach returned to the team for his sophomore year and has led the way so far. The Calgary Flames' fifth-round draft pick leads Quinnipiac with eight points through four games. Wyttenbach hasn’t lost a step from his freshman year, when he finished the season with 59 points.

“(Wyttenbach) is extremely gifted,” Guy Gadowsky said. “He has an unbelievable ability to get behind (the defense) and to make things happen.”

Compared to the entire offense, Wyttenbach is only one part of a well-oiled machine. In its first game of the season, Quinnipiac scored 10 goals in its win against New Hampshire.

Eight Bobcats found the back of the net in their opening game. In total, the high-powered offense scored 21 goals across four games, landing behind No. 2 Michigan with the most goals in the country.

Two Bobcat netminders got the nod in their four games — Christian Kirsch and Rorke Applebee split time for Quinnipiac, with Kirsch logging the better stat line. The freshman allowed only three goals in his two starts and posted a .947 save percentage.

“(Quinnipiac) deserve every bit of credit they did get; they earned it,” Guy Gadowsky said. “They earned the credit from not only last season, but they’ve done it pretty consistently and you have to give it to that whole organization, the whole program, a lot of credit.”

Home opportunity

Luckily for the blue and white, it gets to play the red-hot Bobcats in front of its home crowd for the first time this season. The lone game marks the first of four straight inside Pegula Ice Arena.

Last season, Penn State posted a dominant 14-6 home record. However, it only faced Quinnipiac once heading into this contest, losing 3-2 at the M&T Bank Arena.

Newcomers Kale Dach and Justin Larose finished their first two games in the blue and white with respective goals. They will look to continue their early scoring with their new team in front of a new home.

Both Josh Fleming and Ryder Fetterolf found time between the pipes for Penn State last week. Fleming started for Gadowsky in the season opener, allowing two goals and recording a .917 save percentage. The sophomore will be the primary starter for Penn State throughout the season, with Fetterolf backing him up.

With the roaring home crowd for the season opener, Penn State’s power-play unit will look to not only use the man advantage but also the fans behind them. The Nittany Lions went 0-for-4 on the power play over the weekend.

Ultimately, the four-game home stretch will be an opportunity for Gadowsky and his squad to reset after an unsuccessful start. With the chance, it’s a vital opportunity for other new faces to have their name called for the first time in the blue and white.

title: No. 15 Penn State women’s volleyball hits the road for 2 West Coast conference matches
author: Jimmy Blair | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State may have gotten its campaign back on track.

The blue and white has claimed its last three matches, including a ranked win over No. 20 Washington, and have not lost a set since Oct. 3 in its matchup against Iowa.

The team has performed at an elite level throughout this run. Kennedy Martin has continued to be one of the most prolific talents in the conference.

Her 4.34 kills per set puts her at second in the Big Ten. Paired with Martin is middle blocker Gabrielle Nichols, as her play has ascended to another level this season.

Continuing this stretch of strong form is no doubt the objective of the squad and coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley. It certainly won’t be easy, as the blue and white are set for a road trip across the country for two conference matchups against UCLA and USC, respectively.

UCLA

The Nittany Lions will face the Bruins in Los Angeles on Friday at 10 p.m. The Bruins have been off to a strong start this year, boasting a 13-4 overall record, and are currently 4-2 in the Big Ten. Like the Nittany Lions, they are also coming off three straight victories.

First-year coach Matt Werle has led the Bruins to a strong start this year, while establishing a strong presence in front of the net, as the Bruins rank third in the conference in average blocks per set with 2.86.

Leading the team in this department is middle blocker Marianna Singletary, who leads the conference in blocks with 99 total blocks, 14 of which are single blocks.

The blue and white will have to account for Singletary’s elite play at the net, while using its strong blocking play to kickstart momentum at the net early.

While the Bruins post a strong record, their strength of schedule is noticeably weaker than the Nittany Lions. They have only played against three ranked opponents this year, Kentucky, BYU and Indiana and dropped all three matches.

UCLA will have the home-court advantage of Pauley Pavilion behind them, and the Nittany Lions have played only five matches away from Happy Valley so far this season, posting a 3-2 record in those matches.

USC

The Trojans host the blue and white at 7 p.m. Saturday. They’ve been on a rollercoaster this season with an 8-8 record, and are 2-4 in conference play.

While their suboptimal conference record does paint a picture, the Trojans have fought out wins against ranked opponents such as Arizona State and Indiana. Despite their record, they’re a team that knows they can go toe-to-toe with some of the best squads in the country.

This up-and-down trend continues in their performances. They rank dead last in the conference in hitting percentage, at .202, and are also at the bottom of the Big Ten in points, averaging only 16.78 per set. However, they boast the most blocks in the conference overall with 139.5 total, and average 2.91 blocks per set.

USC puts one of the strongest blocker duos in the country on the floor with Mia Tvrdy and Leah Ford. The duo ranks second and fourth in the conference in average blocks per set, respectively.

Like the Bruins, the Trojans are one of the best blocking teams in the country, and the blue and white will have their work cut out at the net this weekend.

title: Penn State’s men's soccer looks to end winless streak against Northwestern
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State still has the chance to earn its first Big Ten win of the season Friday when the Nittany Lions travel to Northwestern Medicine Field at Martin Stadium.

Northwestern enters Friday’s matchup at 5-5-1 overall after falling 2-1 to No. 14 Washington on Saturday.

The Nittany Lions are 2-7-1 overall and 0-5-1 in Big Ten play after playing Michigan to a scoreless draw on Friday. Penn State is 0-3-1 on the road this season and will look to build on its defensive performance as it searches for its first conference victory.

Penn State leads the all-time series against Northwestern comfortably, but when the teams last met on Oct. 17 last season at Jeffrey Field, they played to a 2-2 draw.

Wildcats look to bounce back

Northwestern has struggled in its last two Big Ten matchups, dropping both games. Before its most recent loss, the Wildcats fell 4-0 to Rutgers on the road in New Jersey. The back-to-back defeats have dropped Northwestern to 2-3 in conference play.

Northwestern is coming off a 2-1 road loss to No. 14 Washington. The Wildcats' lone goal came in the 17th minute when Aaron O’Reilly converted a penalty kick. Northwestern couldn’t find an equalizer, extending its losing streak to two games.

Peter Riesz and Italo Addimandi lead the Wildcats in scoring with four goals each. Addimandi also ranks eighth in the Big Ten in game-winning goals with two. Marco Silva, Bryant Mayer and Tre Barett lead the team in assists with three apiece.

Dominic Pereira has started nine games in goal for Northwestern, allowing 15 goals while recording 31 saves and a .674 save percentage. His 31 saves rank fifth in the Big Ten, while his saves per game rank second.

The Wildcats have also faced red cards this season. Northwestern will look to limit its fouls and rely on its offensive leaders to get back on track against the Nittany Lions.

Nittany Lions continue to search for a conference breakthrough

Penn State is coming off a scoreless draw against Michigan on Friday. The Nittany Lions finished with 14 shots, including four on target, while controlling possession for much of the game. The draw marked the first tie of the season for both teams.

Etienne Reck led Penn State with four shots, putting two on target, while Peter Doran recorded three shots and one shot on goal. Daniel Peluffo-Wiese made three saves to help secure the shutout.

Despite its defensive performance, Penn State remains winless in Big Ten play at 0-5-1. The Nittany Lions will look to build on their performance against Michigan and convert more offensive opportunities into goals.

Penn State is only one spot ahead of Michigan, which is dead last in the Big Ten in goal differential, while the blue and white are last in shots on target, signaling the grueling offensive approach the Nittany Lions have endured.

It has been a rough time for the blue and white as its last win was against Yale on Sept. 4, meaning the Nittany Lions have gone more than a month without a victory. As they look to regain momentum this season, Penn State has a chance to turn things around Friday and earn its first Big Ten win of the season.

title: Column | The Penn State drinking mentality
author: Quentin Jurney | The Daily Collegian
description:
Alcohol and a flourishing college social life are synonymous, and they have been for decades. Even though institutions of higher learning tend to promote their sophisticated educational programs and quality instruction, partying is a massive factor at almost any university in the United States. Penn State specifically has a reputation when it comes to its nightlife. Both Greek life and bars in State College attract large numbers of people to drink on a weekly basis, if not more.

Bars in State College have special events during the week to encourage people to go out and drink — Wednesday karaoke night at the Shandygaff, country night at Bill Pickle’s Tap Room on Tuesday. These themed nights come with discounted drinks, making it even more tempting to go out throughout the week.

With all these deals and parties happening nearly every day of the week, it’s easy to drink every day if you want to; students are enabled to forgo class to drink or get too hungover to attend class the next day.

With this atmosphere surrounding the Penn State campus, alcoholism is a serious worry. Even more worrisome is the mentality surrounding drinking that many students have. I’ve heard many times, “I’m in college, I can’t be an alcoholic,” or "I'm drinking socially and not alone, so it's not a problem.”

Even though people in college can develop alcoholism easily and binge drinking is extremely harmful, people disregard it in college because of the drinking and partying lifestyle that many colleges, including Penn State, offer. It becomes normalized to drink heavily multiple times a week and when you're surrounded by this type of drinking culture, you become desensitized to it.

There are different concerning patterns with drinking, according to the National Institute of Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA): binge drinking and heavy drinking.

Problems with alcohol are often dismissed or disregarded until they become much more serious. The NIAAA defines binge drinking as a pattern of drinking that brings an individual's blood alcohol concentration to 0.08% or higher. For a typical male, this corresponds to consuming five or more drinks in two hours and four or more for females.

A standard drink in the U.S. is considered 12 ounces of beer at 5 percent alcohol by volume, 5 ounces of wine at 12 percent or 1.5 ounces of liquor at 40%. Binge drinking comes with a slew of problems, both short and long-term. These include problems with impairment, such as accidental injury or alcohol poisoning, while the long-term implications are much more concerning. Dependency, higher risk of certain cancers and developmental problems in the brain — especially for those who drink underage.

“Of full-time college students ages 18 to 25, 29.3% reported binge drinking in the past month,” according to the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. A little less than 30 percent of the student population was drinking in a concerningly unhealthy way.

This is a problem at a lot of universities, not just Penn State. Even though there are many ways universities can mitigate the problem, it's still going to happen. I don’t think creating harsher punishments or cracking down on drinking is going to solve the issue. There’s just a societal perception that college and alcohol go hand in hand and it would be very hard to try to change that.

I think most of the responsibility when it comes to drinking should be on the individual student themselves. Of course, the university should try to educate students as much as possible, but there’s only so much one can do to stop a young adult away from home for the first time from trying new things. I think students should take a long, hard look at their drinking and really evaluate their habits.

I don’t see a problem with going out and drinking with your friends in college; that's part of life and it shouldn’t be considered taboo in the slightest, but it’s very easy to go over a proverbial cliff when it comes to drinking and overdoing it. I think there should be more trepidation when it comes to the party culture at Penn State and I think every student needs to reassess their relationship to alcohol before it's too late.

Saying it's only a problem after college is a very dangerous mindset and can lead to lifelong problems. My advice for students: go have fun, drink, go out, be responsibly stupid, but keep yourself in check, know what alcoholism looks like and stop it before it’s something that will haunt you for the rest of your life.

If anyone has trouble with alcoholism, whether it be yourself or someone you know, there’s help available. Even if you don’t want to go to the university or other health services, which is understandable, there’s a confidential hotline: 1-800-662-HELP (4357).

If you or someone you know needs help, please call; you might save a life. We are here for each other and you're never alone.
