title: Penn State’s record-setting White Out was ‘the most crazy feeling’ despite loss to USC
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When “Mo Bamba” by Sheck Wes blared over the loudspeaker, a record-setting crowd shook Beaver Stadium to its core. A hostile choir of eager Penn State fans screamed the song before ditching words to make as much noise as possible in an attempt to throw USC off its game.

That’s the expected volume of a White Out game, but this iteration saw its fair share of firsts on Saturday despite the Trojans defeating the Nittany Lions 31-23.

It was the first White Out game under Campbell, who brought a host of players with him from Iowa State, all of whom got to debut playing in the conditions. 114,419 fans piled into Beaver Stadium, setting the program attendance record, aided by the additional seats offered by the newly constructed west side bleachers.

“It was an unbelievable atmosphere,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “It was one of the most impressive environments that I've been able to coach in or be a part of.”

Campbell voiced his frustration with not being able to deliver a favorable result to the crowd.

He made a similar statement after Penn State’s loss to Wisconsin in the Homecoming game, but the energy brought by the fans had him even more disappointed his team couldn’t get the job done.

“I think the most disappointing part for me is that we can't give this incredible fan base that has shown out,” Campbell said. “We can't give them the result that they deserve, but the reality is we will, and we will find a pathway forward.”

Penn State had been on a two-game skid heading into the White Out game, and Rocco Becht was overjoyed how the fans showed up to support the team in such a manner despite how the season has gone so far.

“Props to all those people, and I appreciate them,” Becht said. “We need all their support as much as we can get for this rest of the season because I know this team's not done. God works in mysterious ways, and that's what we're telling each other right now. We're going to continue to go to work.”

For wide receiver Chase Sowell, he never imagined himself playing in a game like this. He said the crowd noise created the “most crazy feeling.”

“That first snap, first play, the ground was literally shaking,” Sowell said postgame. “Water bottles were shaking.”

Sowell has compared Beaver Stadium to its video game counterpart in EA College Football 27 on multiple occasions, and he said the White Out atmosphere lived up to the expectations.

“Stadium Pulse was on 100,” Sowell said. “It's literally just like the video game. We’ve got a great fanbase. They give us that extra oomph, especially going into like the fourth quarter, third quarter, seeing them around is just like an extra energy bar. The White Out was just different, so it was definitely fun.”

Kicker Ryan Barker said the best part about this particular White Out was seeing the transfers and freshmen experience the atmosphere for the first time.

He and other returning Nittany Lions briefed the newcomers on what to expect Saturday, and Barker said it was great to see them finally experience it, bringing back fond memories.

“I was kind of reliving my first White Out again through the eyes of everyone else,” Barker said.

title: Penn State sees growth offensively, but couldn’t finish in loss to USC
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The result didn’t change from the first two Big Ten games, but the growth in Saturday’s loss to USC pushed the Nittany Lions in a forward direction for the second half of the season.

The Nittany Lions made significant strides in most facets of the game, playing in a much more competitive game compared to its blowout loss to Northwestern in the previous week.

“I would just say tonight, I think we made the right growth,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “I thought we played in a much different rhythm tonight in the football game.”

Rhythm is something Campbell has harped on the last two weeks, saying his team hadn’t fully found it in the first two Big Ten games. Saturday’s loss was different, as the offense kept up with USC’s through a majority of the game.

Despite the loss, the unit garnered the momentum it had been looking for in the past six quarters, scoring more points in the first half than it had in either of the last two games.

“I think we definitely found a rhythm, and that's credit to coach (Taylor Mouser) and credit to Rocco,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “I think they did a great job of staying within the game plan, not trying to force anything, taking what they give us. So yeah, I definitely think we took a step forward.”

Although the run game didn’t generate much with only 2.2 yards per carry, it was utilized to set up the pass game, which Penn State had a lot more success with than the previous week.

The ability to use the run game to find success through the air added to the complexity of Penn State’s offense and kept it in the flow of the game.

“When you talk about the ability to use the run game to set up the pass game, play action passing, movement passing, I think all those things were realities tonight,” Campbell said.

Rocco Becht recognized the team’s ability to show fight in a game where the Trojans continued to throw punches in their pass game.

The offensive response to USC’s scores was part of the growth Campbell saw, as it kept the Nittany Lions in contention throughout the duration of the game.

“I felt like we just kept playing no matter what happened,” Becht said. “We went down 7-0 early and we were able to drive the ball right down the field and we did it again.”

Becht led the offense to three scoring drives in the first half, matching USC en route to a 17-17 halftime score. That in itself was an improvement from the week prior, where Northwestern led 24-7 at the half and the offense couldn’t respond to the Wildcats’ punches.

“I think the tenacity and the conviction that we had today was a lot better,” Becht said. “But we just got to be able to finish the games and we're not doing that right now.”

The strides the Nittany Lions made didn’t change the result of the game, however, with the team coming up short in the fourth quarter on both sides of the ball. That part of the game is what stood out to the players.

The Nittany Lions made progress but couldn’t put it all together to come out victorious.

“Still got a long way to go,” offensive lineman Trevor Buhr said. “I honestly feel like we had a great week of preparation. Just came up short.”

Penn State took a step it hadn’t taken in almost two games, finding momentum and competing with the No. 19 team in the country. It didn’t get the result it wanted on the scoreboard, but the play on the field was more of the production from the first three games of the season rather than the first two games of conference play.

“I did think there were some moments tonight where we grew a lot closer to the team that we want to be than where we were, especially last week,” Campbell said.

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's loss to USC
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
A record-setting crowd of 114,419 fans packed in Beaver Stadium on Saturday night as Penn State returned home to face No. 19 USC in the Nittany Lions’ first White Out game under Matt Campbell.

While the game was tied, 17-17, at halftime, the Trojans continued to exploit Penn State’s failing secondary and ran away with a 31-23 victory. The Nittany Lions fell to 3-3 overall and 0-3 in the Big Ten while USC improved to 6-1 overall and 3-1 in the conference.

Here are three takeaways from Penn State’s loss to USC.

Penn State’s identity is a pass-first team

Campbell said Tuesday he felt his team “lacked an identity.” Rocco Becht said Campbell didn’t quite know whether the offense was pass-first or run-first.

That question was answered on Saturday, as Becht came out of the gates swinging with an offense closely mirroring how the team played in the nonconference schedule. Becht went 21-for-32 for 289 passing yards with a touchdown.

“I thought Rocco certainly gave us every opportunity in the football game to be successful,” Campbell said postgame. “He found a rhythm that we want to play in, and that we need to continue to move forward in for sure.”

Penn State’s second play of the game was a 47-yard completion to wide receiver Chase Sowell. But unlike his poor performance against Northwestern, Becht continued to find success in the passing game, particularly utilizing his deep ball and looked like his early-season self, showing poise in the pocket and delivering accurate and timely passes.

A few of the incompletions weren’t on him, either, as both running back James Peoples and Rappleyea dropped open checkdown passes. Becht did sail a throw through the back of the end zone that was intended for tight end Benjamin Brahmer in the fourth quarter, so it wasn’t all perfect through the air.

“Not good enough. I think for me, like I've always said, I'm a perfectionist, and I need to be better,” Becht said. “I felt like we took a small step today, but we just got to be able to finish.”

There was a bigger emphasis on the tight end room as well, primarily coming from Rappleyea, who had the most targets and Penn State’s only receiving touchdown.

Saturday’s offensive performance showed Penn State can be explosive even without star wide receiver Koby Howard, as Sowell finished with 95 yards while seven players had a catch.

Becht’s legs open new possibilities

Becht’s ability to run the football was nowhere to be found through the first five weeks of the season. But he unlocked that piece of his game in front of the largest crowd in Beaver Stadium history, finishing the game with 20 yards on 10 carries.

Penn State’s offensive line gave Becht the time and space to rush up the middle, and his brief instances of success were crucial on fourth down specifically, as he twice called his own number to move the chains.

“He is a good runner and he can make plays with his legs,” running back Carson Hansen said. “We have seen him do it in the past.”

One such run was a 10-yard gain on a fourth-and-3 in the dying moments of the second quarter. He recognized the advancing Trojan defense and sprinted to the right for the first down, running out of bounds with three seconds on the clock. The gain paved the way for kicker Ryan Barker to tie the game before the half with a 48-yard field goal.

He wasn’t just mobile beyond the line of scrimmage. Becht demonstrated a key ability to throw on the run on play action, headlined by an impressive 37-yard completion to Sowell in the second quarter.

Utilizing Becht’s legs in the offense proved how effective Penn State’s ground game can be when it’s not just the running backs carrying the ball. Should the running backs establish a stronger run game, Becht’s mobility adds an extra layer for opposing defenses to consider when scouting the Nittany Lions.

Secondary falls apart

Penn State’s secondary — particularly the cornerbacks — have been the team’s best unit so far this season. USC broke that trend as quarterback Jayden Maiava threw for 301 yards and three touchdowns.

The run defense, which was the problem against Northwestern, only allowed 129 yards by comparison.

Wide receivers Trent Mosley and Tanook Hines were left wide open on nearly every play, despite Penn State’s pass rush sometimes only sending three rushers. Additionally, the Trojans had 86 yards after catch as the Nittany Lions once again struggled to tackle at an elite level.

“(Maiava’s) a super talented passer,” defensive end Caleb Bacon said. “Struggled a little bit there to keep (the passing game) contained because we knew he can make those throws outside the pocket on the move and hit open receivers. We really knew that coming in. This could be the best group of outside skill receivers that we were going to see.”

D’Anton Lynn spoke extensively about Penn State’s poor tackling at Northwestern, and he increased the number of tackling drills at practice this week in hopes of fixing that. However, the Nittany Lions, except for Tony Rojas, once again struggled to tackle at some points.

Penn State’s tackling is a serious issue, more now than ever, as the secondary wasn’t able to threaten USC’s receivers.

title: Penn State White Out game against USC breaks Beaver Stadium attendance record

title: 'We need to give Campbell time' | Penn State students, fans share thoughts on state of the program
author: Andrew Deal & Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State didn’t begin Big Ten play the way it wanted to, going 0-2 in the conference so far with losses to Wisconsin and Northwestern, leading to ticket prices plummeting for the White Out game against USC on Saturday.

Here’s what Penn State students and fans had to say about the program, football leadership and ticket prices ahead of the Nittany Lions’ signature game.

State of the program

Fans have mixed reactions about the current state of the program, with Penn State currently sitting at 3-2 on the year.

The Nittany Lions are mixing players from their team last year with players from Matt Campbell’s squad at Iowa State in 2025, in addition to players from around the country.

“Can't have Iowa State guys on a Big Ten team, right?” Alex Fielding, Class of 2026, said. “It's not going to work. The Big Ten's way different. It's like throwing an ACC school in the SEC.”

The program was coming off two seasons where it had national championship caliber rosters — with 2024 ending in the College Football Playoff semifinals and 2025 unraveling to a 7-6 season. In Campbell’s first year, there were some high expectations similar to the previous two years, especially considering the weaker schedule.

The first two Big Ten games didn’t show that with losses to Northwestern and Wisconsin, and fans felt that hit just like the team did.

“We're used to being a perennial team that is competing in the top-10 year in and year out, and so all of a sudden we get slapped in the face,” Nicholas Pajovich, a fifth-year student studying landscape contracting said.

Zach Sherry, a third-year student studying animal science, understood it was going to be a process and there were going to be growing pains. The process also came with a new apparel partner and a $700 million stadium renovation that’s set to finish in 2027, adding to the long-term plan of the program, rather than more focus on the short term.

“I didn't have expectations that were super high, so (Campbell) coming from the Big 12, there's not much competition over there, to say the least,” Sherry said. “They have a couple good teams, but it's not in-depth as the Big Ten is like Ohio State, Michigan, so I knew that it would take a transition period.”

Pat Kraft

Over the past week, there have been a lot of thoughts online about Penn State Vice President for Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft.

A lot of it stems from the way Kraft handled the coaching search, which many fans weren’t very fond of.

“I'm disappointed in how he went about hiring a coach for Penn State,” Sherry said. “I feel like he took way too long. It all comes down to recruiting. Campbell didn't have enough time to recruit because Pat Kraft waited so long to hire a coach.”

Fielding also brought up how important recruiting is, noting that a majority of Franklin’s 2026 recruiting class followed him to Virginia Tech.

“I think that was going to happen inevitably, but I think losing all the guys in the middle of the season was the worst thing for us,” Fielding said. “We need to keep those guys and all the recruits. If we fire him at the end of the year, we don't lose those recruits, and we have Penn State players instead of Iowa State players.”

After Franklin was fired, it was almost a two-month process before the Nittany Lions hired Campbell to be the next coach. That process brought multiple speculatory coaches as other targets before Kraft honed in on Campbell.

Kraft’s decisions in the hiring process have Jacob Figuera, a first-year business student, questioning his Penn State football fandom.

“He's dropping the ball and as a team we can't be making those mistakes,” Figuera said. “I think it's embarrassing. I'm embarrassed to say I'm a Penn State student when it comes to football.”

Matt Campbell

One of the reasons for Franklin’s firing was because he had a poor track record of winning the biggest games, going 4-21 against AP top-10 opponents. However, Franklin generally won the games he was projected to win, making Penn State a routinely winning program.

Campbell stepped into a role where fans had grown accustomed to the Nittany Lions’ winning ways, and hasn’t brought the same consistency against unranked opponents Franklin did. But Pajovich said fans are “spoiled,” and need to be patient as Franklin finished his first season at Penn State 7-6 in 2015.

“Campbell got himself in very big shoes to fill,” Pajovich said. “As Penn State fans, we had it very good for those for the last decade that we had Franklin, and that success didn't happen immediately. We need to give Campbell time.”

Dylan Tollini, a third-year student studying photojournalism, noted the stark differences between Campbell and Franklin’s coaching philosophies. While Franklin was announced in the team’s lineup every game and led the team entrance off the bus, Campbell let the players take the spotlight.

“(Campbell’s) definitely the opposite of Franklin,” Tollini said. “Campbell was like nowhere to be seen, and that was nice.”

Brian Silfies, 47, said although he believes the hiring search "misfired," he still thinks Campbell’s the right person for the job. He cited how his coaching philosophy emphasizes building strong character first and foremost.

“Campbell was a good pick, especially for the old-school Penn State people, the players being good people and stuff like that,” Silfies said. “It’s more like the (Joe) Paterno way.”

Ticket prices, attendance ahead of White Out

Silfies and his father Ronald, 72, have been season-ticket holders for the past 15 years. Seeing as White Out tickets have plummeted after Penn State dropped two games, Silfies voiced his grievances.

“As a season ticket holder, that sucks because then you think about how my ticket was $200 and somebody's buying it for $60,” Silfies said.

But the Silfies family doesn’t put the blame wholly on the team. Ronald said he’s concerned about how the renovations to Beaver Stadium are impacting the prices of tickets, especially for those in the west side.

The announced attendance at the Wisconsin game was 108,014, however there were many unclaimed seats in the new upper west side. Ronald noted how older fans won’t want to sit there not only because of the price, but also because it’s “way too steep.”

“They're going to have a hard time filling the west side because of the prices on those tickets,” Ronald said. “The people that have been going here for 50 years can't afford to keep those seats anymore. It's a shame.”

title: Key DT game-time decision for Penn State ahead of USC

title: Penn State’s women’s cross country sees multiple improvements in Nuttycombe Invitational
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State continued its postseason preparation at the Nuttycombe Invitational in Madison, Wisconsin, finishing 14th in a 33-team field. The Nittany Lions competed against a deep field of 222 finishers, including 18 nationally ranked women’s teams.

The No. 29 Penn State women’s cross country team finished ahead of three nationally ranked programs: No. 23 Washington, No. 24 Providence and No. 30 Boise State. The Nittany Lions also finished just three points behind No. 21 Minnesota and seven points behind No. 11 Stanford.

Penn State placed third among the eight Big Ten teams competing in the invitational. Northwestern led the conference with its 11th-place finish, followed by Minnesota in 13th and Penn State in 14th.

Multiple Nittany Lions improved on their previous season-best times, showing progress as the team continued its postseason preparation.

As the race began, freshman Vivian Kipruto led the Nittany Lions through the opening 2k, crossing the marker in 45th place in 6:34.8. Senior Claire Zubey followed in 62nd with a time of 6:36.8.

Graduate student Katie Dallas and sophomore Caroline Tribett finished 94th and 105th, respectively, as Penn State established its position in the competitive field.

By the 4k mark, Kipruto had moved up seven spots into 38th place, continuing to establish herself among the field’s top finishers. Dallas also made significant progress, climbing 12 places to 82nd, while Tribett moved into 92nd.

Zubey dropped to 74th despite a strong opening stretch, and sophomore Eva Kynaston improved 15 places to 113th place.

As the race approached the finish, the Nittany Lions saw a mix of late-race movement across the lineup. Dallas continued her climb, moving into 77th place, while Zubey finished 79th after reaching 74th at the 4k checkpoint.

Kipruto ultimately led Penn State across the finish line, placing 39th with a time of 20:11.0. The freshman improved significantly on her previous season and personal best time of 20:45.4, cutting more than 34 seconds off her mark.

Dallas finished next for the blue and white in 77th place with a time of 20:38.0, improving upon her previous season best of 20:47.8. Zubey followed closely in 79th, finishing in 20:39.3 to lower her season-best time by nearly four seconds.

Kynaston crossed the line in 111th place in 20:57.4, narrowly surpassing her previous season-best of 20:59.6. Tribett finished 118th in 21:00.2.

At the same time, graduate student Charlotte Costich finished 127th in 21:03.6, improving by nearly 19 seconds on her previous season-best of 21:22.5. Freshman Reese Miller rounded out the Penn State lineup, finishing 157th in 21:13.5.

Florida junior Judy Chepkoech won the individual race in 19:19.5, leading the field in a meet that featured some of the top individual runners and nationally ranked programs in collegiate cross country.

With multiple runners improving on their season-best performances, the Nittany Lions secured 14th place overall among 33 teams.

Up next

Both teams' next race will be Friday, October 16th, at 11 a.m. at the NCAA Pre-National Invitational in Terre Haute, Indiana.

MORE CROSS COUNTRY COVERAGE

title: No. 18 Penn State women's volleyball sweeps Northwestern
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
There was a buzz in the air Friday night as Penn State handily defeated Northwestern in a 3-0 sweep to kickoff White Out weekend.

The atmosphere in the arena was electric to kickoff the match, with many alumni and current students in attendance for the THON match. This electricity helped Penn State to a 25- 18 first-set win that Penn State dominated at the start with a combination of good net play and striking.

Still, Northwestern came back after multiple kills by Campbell Paris and Maya Stillwell, along with missed volleys and inaccurate shots.

The standout of the first set was true freshman Kendall Northern, who tallied five kills in the opening frame. Kennedy Martin also had a strong first set, tallying four kills, including one to end the set.

The second half started tight as the Nittany Lions and Wildcats traded 4 errors with the score at 8-8 to start the frame. Northwestern's libero Lauren Dignan played well for the Wildcats in this set, totaling eight digs and keeping it close.

The momentum then shifted on a service ace by Alexis Stucky that then led to a run of three straight kills by Kennedy Martin to push the score to 19-12 in the set alongside Whitney Lauenstein, who had 4 kills, one being the final point, giving the Nittany Lions a second-set victory 25 to 17.

The Nittany Lions started the third set hot, leading 7-2 after multiple kills and a service ace by Ava Faduto, as Haley Burgdof and Gabrielle Nichols showed impressive striking ability. Things got even better for Penn State after the lead was extended to 18-10 after more offensive dominance by Nichols. Northwestern then closed the gap dramatically after multiple aces by Gigi Navarette and a slew of errors by Penn State's rotational players, cutting the deficit to 18-17.

After that, the dynamic duo of Alexis Stucky and Martin came in; Martin proved strong, tallying three kills when she entered in leading the Nittany Lions to the finish line, winning the set 25-19 on a strong kill by Northern.

Overall, Penn State played well in this conference matchup and will have a chance to build on the momentum of a strong sweep victory.

Northern finished the game with a .923 hitting percentage and 12 kills, which is a new career high. Martin only slightly edged the freshman with 15 kills, while posting the next-highest hitting percentage in the match at .560.

With the result, the blue and white have now won back-to-back contests, improving to 11-4 and 3-2 in conference play ahead of its ranked weekend matchup. The blue and white are now tied with Michigan State, UCLA, Indiana and Illinois in conference standings. After 10 games at Rec Hall this season, Penn State has dropped only two, both to squads that outranked Penn State in the AVCA Poll.

Up next

Penn State returns to Rec Hall for a Big Ten matchup against Washington at noon on Sunday.

title: Penn State men’s soccer earns scoreless draw against Michigan
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a devastating last-minute 2-1 loss to Ohio State, Penn State traveled to Ann Arbor to face the Michigan Wolverines in a conference matchup. Neither team has won a Big Ten matchup and is looking for its first.

The Nittany Lions entered Friday's matchup at 2-7, while Michigan struggled to 3-4-2. Both teams came into this game with a loss and had a chance to turn their seasons around.

Despite Penn State's offensive pressure, the game ended in a scoreless draw.

First half

The Wolverines came out attacking early, but the Nittany Lions stopped them early and had a counterattack of their own. While unsuccessful, Penn State was able to stay in the Michigan attack third for a bit.

Michigan got a break once they cleared the ball out and created a chance of their own. Michigan attackers flooded the box, and both teams scrambled for possession, but the Penn State defense was able to clear it out.

Etienne Reck followed the ball out, dribbled up the field, and created a shot opportunity for himself just outside the box in the seventh minute. But Isaiah Golden made the save, punching the ball out-of-bounds.

This was Golden's first save of the season after returning from injury.

As a result, Michigan won a corner kick, which the defense cleared out. The offense then turned to over with Alex Gimple, who took a shot in the bottom center of the net, but Penn State goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese saved it.

In the 10th minute, Reck pushed the attack and got another shot off, but yet again it was off target.

Finally, in the 15th minute, Michigan's Guy Michaeli took a shot, but the ball was blocked. Wolverines earned a corner but could not get a shot off, and Will Baker fouled Joe Sheridan, throwing off the Michigan offense.

The Wolverines got right back on the attack as Grayson Elmquist took a shot out wide. Elmquist applied pressure to the Penn State defense for the first time in a while.

As the blue and white attacked once again, Amadou Kone was able to draw a foul in the midfield, earning the team a free kick. The ball was played into the box, but the offense could do nothing with it.

The physical match carried on; there were four fouls in two minutes, three for Penn State and one for Michigan through the 21st and 23rd minutes.

After a back-and-forth between the teams, Reck made another break through with his third shot of the night that was blocked, earning the team back-to-back corners. Grant McIntosh was able to earn a shot but was headed out by Will Baker.

In the 38th minute, Vladislav Cherny took a shot but missed; shortly after, Arian Recinos took a shot of his own and also missed.

Throughout the game, Michigan struggled in midfield and with ball possession. The Wolverines turned the ball over countless times in the midfield, preventing any attack.

The first yellow card of the game was given to Reck for unsportsmanlike behavior in the 43rd minute.

After Penn State dominated offensively and Michigan struggled, it ended in a scoreless half.

Second half

The offensive domination for Penn State continued, allowing Kone to take a shot off within a minute of the half.

Once Michigan transitioned, Noah Andreas pushed Michaeli in the back and earned the second yellow card of the game in the 47th minute.

Michigan counterattacked after a Penn State slip-up as Michaeli got a shot off that was blocked in the 49th minute.

Penn State continued to pressure to the Michigan defense, trying to score, but were still unsuccessful.

In the 61st minute, the Wolverines created an attack opportunity of their own and applied pressure to the box, with the Michigan offense crowding it. Peluffo-Wiese saved Jake Tatch's shot on frame. Michigan scrambled for the rebound, and Michael Ramirez took the shot but missed.

Reck continued his offensive presence with another shot in the 64th minute, but Goldson made a diving save. Peter Doran came in shortly after and took a shot, but it was blocked as well.

Nico Pendleton cleared out the ball for Michigan as Penn State scrambled to get a shot off.

Doran took a nasty hit and was subbed off after a supposed head injury in the 72nd minute.

Both teams took turns attacking and getting shots off, but ultimately the game ended in a tie.

Up next

Penn State returns to action Tuesday at home against Rutgers at 7 p.m.

MORE SOCCER COVERAGE

title: No. 17 Penn State men's hockey drops season opener to No. 16 UConn
author: Dominic Megats I The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s been over a year since former Nittany Lion Matt DiMarsico sent Penn State to the Frozen Four after finding the back of the net in overtime against UConn.

Fast-forward to the present day, only seven players on the current roster were a part of that infamous game. The rest are young and hungry players looking to get the blue and white back in that position.

The first challenge in Penn State’s way was a Huskies team with revenge in their mind. A team with several new additions couldn’t get past first-game mistakes, leading to a 3-1 loss to No. 16 UConn in its season opener.

The Nittany Lions rolled with Shea Van Olm, Dane Dowiak and Maine transfer Justin Poirier to open the game. Jackson Smith and Mac Gadowsky paired at the blue line for Game 1 of the Ice Breaker Tournament.

Penn State’s first quality chance on UConn netminder Kam Hendrickson came from a one-timer attempt by Andrew Kuzma to Kale Dach, who was parked in front of the net. Ultimately, the sophomore made the save, springing the Huskies' forecheck.

Will McIsaac used the spark from his goalie to open the scoring for UConn after ripping a wrist shot from the right faceoff circle through a screen. This goal marked the freshman’s first collegiate goal.

After spending the majority of the opening period attacking, the Nittany Lions found themselves down early as they continued to feel out their new lines.

Despite the continuous offensive pressure that lasted until the horn sounded, the blue and white headed into the locker room down 1-0 after the first period of its season.

Penn State continued its relentless pressure to open the second period. Every opportunity continued to be shut down by Hendrickson.

That changed when Dach found the back of the net off a backhand through a net-front scrum. The freshman’s first collegiate goal proved to be a much-needed tie after several empty chances.

Shortly after the first goal of the season for the Nittany Lions, the power-play unit was tested after Reese Laubach was checked from behind and into the boards.

After finishing sixth in the Big Ten in power-play percentage, Penn State couldn’t capitalize on its first man advantage of the season.

Penalties weren’t one-sided as Justin Larose committed his first collegiate penalty, putting the Huskies on the man advantage with eight minutes left in the middle period. The blue and white tightened its defense and earned a late penalty kill.

UConn didn’t take the failed power-play lightly as Alexandre Blais found Joey Muldowney in the slot, leading to a rocket of a shot that beat Josh Fleming.

The late goal killed the momentum for the blue and white, ending the second period in the defensive zone and heading into the intermission down 2-1.

Penn State returned to the man advantage only four minutes into the third period. The crucial late chance to tie the game was for nothing as the Huskies stayed ahead.

Both offenses found a spark halfway through the final frame. The two sides had a couple of pristine chances. Fleming was tested most in the flurry after making a sprawling glove save to keep the lead to just one goal.

Poirier believed he had the game-tying goal for the blue and white until the Huskies' challenge for goaltender interference was successful, keeping the 2-1 lead intact.

With just under three minutes left in the game, Guy Gadowsky pulled Fleming to use an extra attacker in an effort to tie the contest late.

The added attacker was answered by a Kaden Shahan empty-net goal to seal a 3-1 UConn win over the Nittany Lions.

Up next

Penn State heads to Martire Family Ice Arena to face Sacred Heart for Game 2 of the Ice Breaker Tournament.

MORE HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: No. 4 Penn State women's hockey upset in thrilling overtime loss to Syracuse
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions traveled to Syracuse, New York, for their first road match of the season against the Syracuse Orange.

Penn State fell in a 5-4 upset after battling back from a 2-0 and 4-2 deficit to the Orange for their first loss to an unranked opponent this season.

The Nittany Lions had won 11 straight games against Syracuse prior to the loss. The blue and white will head into the second leg of the series hoping to make up for the defeat.

First period

The opening two minutes were back-and-forth with neither team controlling the puck in their offensive zone. Grace Tullock caused the first stoppage of the game with a shot from the right side that the Orange goaltender Ava Drabyk saved.

After being called for tripping, Syracuse gave up their first power play of the day. Penn State fired multiple shots, but the Orange penalty kill blocked many attempts.

Both defenses were showing up early, as each side allowed only one shot in the first eight minutes. Yet, Penn State earned themselves more opportunities to set up their offense.

Syracuse didn’t need to set up their offense, as Jackson Kinsler scored on a breakaway goal which was assisted by Emma Gnade. The Orange won the puck in their defensive zone and raced down the ice.

Following the goal, Syracuse continued to hound the Nittany Lions defensively. The blue and white pushed through, continuing to let off shots. With four minutes left in the period, Penn State led 14-7 in shots.

Mikah Keller added to the count on a one-on-one breakaway, but Drabyk denied her.

Unable to score, Penn State left the 1st period down 1-0.

Second period

Syracuse continued to show its grit within the opening minutes of the second period. While the Nittany Lions held the puck in the offensive zone, they couldn’t generate any quality looks.

A holding penalty on Danica Maynard, followed by an interference by Rachel Walsh, led to an even four-on-four play. The Orange stood tall and killed their second penalty of the game, as Penn State still couldn’t find its footing offensively.

With 11 minutes left in the period, Penn State led the Orange with 33 shots compared to their nine. However, Ava Drabyk had completely owned the crease up to this point with 21 saves.

The officials sent Jessica Cheung to the penalty box for boarding, giving the Nittany Lions their third power play of the game. Ava Drabyk made another incredible save, diving across the goal to stop a shot, adding to a stellar performance and ending the Penn State power play.

After a timeout, Syracuse misses its initial breakaway attempt, but after a scrum for the puck in front of the crease, Jordan Blouin finds her stick on the puck for a goal of her own. She extended their lead to 2-0.

Penn State, which had sent 31 shots on goal, finally connected on a goal by Sophie Morrow. It had seemed inevitable for the Nittany Lions to send one past Drabyk.

The goal gave Penn State the momentum it needed, as Mikah Keller tied the game after taking the puck down the ice and setting up the breakaway. The blue and white tied it at 2-2.

Third period

Two minutes into the final frame, Stickney cleared the puck right into the path of a Syracuse attacker, but immediately made up for the mistake by saving the shot.

Following a defensive stop on their defensive end, the Orange cleared the puck and Nea Tervonen sped past two Nittany Lion defenders to receive that puck. She would miss her 1-on-1 opportunity but stayed with the rebound and scored to regain the lead at 3-2.

Syracuse immediately earned a power play after Mckenna Walsh was called for delay of game. The momentum swung back in the Orange’s favor as Jocelyn Fiala scored a long-distance one-time shot to push the lead to two.

A hooking call sent Alara Murphy to the penalty box, giving Penn State another power play opportunity. Danica Maynard scored a much-needed goal after receiving the rebound off of Drabyk’s pads. The blue and white cut their deficit to 4-3.

During the final minutes of the final frame, both sides played aggressive defense, not allowing the opposing attack to set their offense. Yet the Nittany Lions’ relentlessness led to another comeback after falling behind by two goals. Nicole Hall scored from the right side to tie it 4-4.

Stickney made two clutch saves with two minutes left. A clearance off of the side wall deflected to a Syracuse attacker, leading to a one-on-one shot attempt. Then, the Orange had a great look in the middle of the ice that couldn’t get past the freshman.

Neither team could score with time winding down, and the two teams headed into overtime tied at 4-4.

Overtime

Kampersal decided to switch goaltenders, as Maddy Campbell entered the game. The decision proved costly when Jocelyn Fiala sent a shot over Campbell's head and into the back of the net to upset the Nittany Lions, 5-4.

Up next

Penn State closes out its series against Syracuse tomorrow at 3 p.m.

MORE HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: Penn State field hockey defeats Michigan State 1-0 in overtime, Gaitan delivers final blow
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
After Penn State’s 3-2 overtime win over Lafayette on Sunday, the Nittany Lions entered a stretch of the season dominated by Big Ten conference play. That stretch kicked off with a head-to-head battle in East Lansing against the Michigan State Spartans on Friday.

Ultimately, the Nittany Lions came away with the 1-0 overtime win over Michigan State, extending their winning streak to four games.

Heading into this matchup, the blue and white faced a schedule where six out of seven of its remaining regular season games are against conference opponents. Coach Hannah Prince knew her hands would be full with the postseason looming large soon.

The opening minutes of the first quarter were fairly balanced for both teams as physical defending and fouls became the norm.

The Spartan defense kept Penn State out of their entire back half of the field for the first five minutes of action.

With 8:18 remaining in the first, sophomore defensive back Cooper Cutchins took the first shot for the Nittany Lions, but it sailed just wide of the net.

Much of the first quarter was dominated by Michigan State, forcing Penn State to make costly mistakes in their own defensive half of the field that stripped away their chances of gaining early momentum.

The Nittany Lions got their first real shot on goal with just over three minutes remaining off an attempt from redshirt freshman midfielder Hope Russo, but it proved unsuccessful.

Penn State ended the first 15 minutes of play without a single goal or penalty corner for the second straight game this season.

The beginning of the second quarter was the same in terms of offensive output for the Nittany Lions, but their ball movement within the seams became more crisp and direct.

Sophomore forward Lara Pyle’s shot went left and wide of the net with just under 11 minutes remaining in the first half, and the score remained 0-0.

Neither the Spartans nor the Nittany Lions gave up a penalty corner chance as the halfway point of the second quarter passed.

Penn State’s first penalty corner came with 5:55 remaining in the first half. Sophomore forward Joji Purdy’s two shots were both blocked by the Spartan defense.

The Nittany Lions were given a second penalty corner just seconds later, but that too proved unsuccessful, and the score remained 0-0.

At the 3:30 mark of the second quarter, Michigan State still had put up zero shots on goal.

The closing minutes of the first half saw lots of turnovers on both sides and left both teams scoreless despite the solid ball movement from both Michigan State and Penn State.

Penn State began the third quarter wasting no time getting into the Spartan inner circle, but couldn’t convert its first points.

With 12:43 remaining, Purdy’s shot sailed wide left of the net, and the Nittany Lions led Michigan State 7-0 in total shots.

Penn State’s third penalty corner came with 12 minutes remaining. Graduate midfielder Camryn Standish’s shot was deflected by the Michigan State defense and ultimately stopped by junior goalkeeper Lola Munoz de Verger.

The first half of the third quarter saw the Nittany Lions take most of the time of possession away from the Spartans.

Michigan State earned its first penalty corner with 7:22 remaining. Penn State’s defense held strong and stopped the scoring opportunity.

de Verger’s key save for the Spartans with just under five minutes remaining stopped the Nittany Lion fast break, which was their best chance at taking the lead.

Both teams continued their solid defense of their respective halves of the field, resulting in both sides remaining scoreless heading into the final quarter of regulation.

The first few minutes of the fourth quarter were consumed with fouls for both sides, with the ball constantly changing hands seemingly every couple of seconds.

The Nittany Lions earned their fourth penalty corner with 9:05 remaining in regulation. Junior forward Ella Gaitan’s shot was sent back by de Verger.

Freshman forward Chloe D’Hage’s attempt was also knocked away by the Spartan defense, and the scoring stalemate continued.

Graduate midfielder Sienna Dunn and Pyle’s attempts were sent back by de Verger with 6:20 remaining.

The Nittany Lions had yet another corner opportunity with 6:12 remaining, resulting in no goal once again.

Penn State was given an eighth penalty corner with 3:50 remaining, but the ball rolled out of the circle before Penn State took a shot on goal.

Michigan State’s potential game-winning goal was called off, sending the game to overtime and marking the Nittany Lions’ second-straight extra time contest.

To begin the sudden death overtime, Penn State wasted little time. The blue and white scored the game-winning goal off a shot from Gaitan, giving the blue and white their second-straight overtime win.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions will face Kent State in Ohio at noon Sunday.

title: Former Penn State RB Kaytron Allen claimed by Miami Dolphins
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:

title: Penn State men’s basketball notebook | Mike Rhoades, Brant Byers, Ivan Jurić speak at Big Ten Media Day
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
The cagers commanded Chicago on Thursday.

With Penn State’s return to the hardwood less than two weeks away, the blue and white traveled to the Windy City for Big Ten Media Day. Transfer addition Brant Byers and returning 7-footer Ivan Jurić joined Mike Rhoades for a segment where they fielded questions about the upcoming season.

Here’s a recap of what the trio said during the presser, streamed on the Big Ten Network.

Addressing the noise

While Rhoades spoke extensively about his team’s struggles last season through multiple media availabilities up to the season, he echoed similar sentiments on the national scene about why things didn’t pan out.

“We just didn't have enough toughness, enough grit, couldn't draw the line in the sand at times in Big Ten play,” Rhoades said. “We hung in there with people, but there was just not enough and we went out there and found it. We got some older guys, we got some bigger, tougher guys — that's important.”

Rhoades has been firm on the physical aspect of this year’s Nittany Lions, something signaled during the squad’s open practice earlier this offseason. While Rhoades claims to have patched that physicality, he also noted the intangibles that this year’s unit has compared to the season prior.

“Maybe not as deep as the rest of the league, but I like our group, and we had to address that,” Rhoades said. “The character of competition and the character of toughness. We needed that for sure.”

Jurić shared a similar opinion to Rhoades with needing to add physicality and toughness. He explained that after his first year, he learned the pace, physicality and athleticism of the Big Ten. The Zagreb, Croatia, native noted his weight room work and striving toward consistency, something Byers also expressed when detailing his transfer to Happy Valley.

“Build the habits of being tough, and then make it a behavior, and get to a point where that's just what we do,” Rhoades said. “We have to overachieve at Penn State. It is what it is in the Big Ten for us — I'm cool with that, I'm excited about that. But we have to have a level of toughness and grit and fight to find a way to overachieve on a Saturday night on the road in the Big Ten.”

Big man on campus

When Byers made his decision to use the portal to transfer from Miami (OH) to Penn State, it was widely signaled as a major move for the program.

The Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, native averaged 14.2 points per game behind his silky shot from beyond the arc and was part of a RedHawks squad that went undefeated in the regular season and, despite losing in the MAC Tournament quarterfinals, made an NCAA Tournament appearance.

“If we were going to bring anybody in, they had to fit me, and they had to hit that toughness barometer, as we called it. But also from winning programs, culture programs that know what it looks like and what it feels like,” Rhoades said. “Brant went through that last year at a high level, and he's a big part of it.”

Byers and Jurić repeated Rhoades’ idea of bringing those past values to help the current squad, bringing over people who “know how to win.” Yet for Byers it wasn’t just knowing how to bring home Ws that made him appealing to Penn State, but rather local ties.

“I mean it's pretty special, it's kind of a dream come true in a way,” Byers said. “Just thinking back to the players growing up that I would watch playing at Penn State, I think it's pretty crazy that I now have that Penn State logo on myself. Get to wear that jersey as well. It's pretty special — I'm pretty lucky.”

Byers shared some of the love to one of his teammates, Dasonte Bowen, for his work as a veteran vocal leader and detailed the intersquad belief that runs through the Penn State locker rooms for themselves and coaching.

“He's happy he's with us, and it makes me happy when he hits those long threes, that's for sure,” Rhoades said. “But really appreciate his approach and the type of teammate he is, and he's gone off to a great start.”

Rhoades or Bonaparte?

While the Penn State boss talked about those additions, it’s clear that there’s an underlying commonality among those newcomers donning blue and white — international roots.

The Nittany Lions have six fresh players coming from overseas, five of whom were European-born. Rhoades said Penn State “opened the door” for the new Euro-blood and described how the blue and white handled the new approach.

“Brent Scott, my associate coach, played 15 years in Europe; Taylor Battle, maybe one of the best players we ever had, He played 10 years in Europe — They know people, they know agents,” Rhoades said. “Those doors we're keeping them wide open, and we're finding we're building some great relationships … there's basketball players all over the world. You just got to go find them and then get them excited about your place.”

Rhoades made imprints all over the continent this offseason. Penn State landed Tim Oboh from England, François Wibaut from France, Roberts Blums from Latvia and Balkan forwards Aleksandar Zečević and Roko Prkačin.

“I'm really excited about Roko Prkačin; Roko is a very versatile player… Francois is like a Big Ten wing, big, physical, strong guy, can guard multiple positions and Robert Blums, who transferred from Davidson, a winning culture program, is going to give us a lot,” Rhoades said. “We went out and got different guys from all over the world, but guys that love to play basketball and love to compete, and it's really helped us. It's been fun coaching these guys — I can't wait to get started.”

title: Penn State women’s volleyball continues homestand, hosting Northwestern, Iowa
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State continues conference play following its 3-1 win against Iowa on Saturday. The Nittany Lions will face Northwestern at 7:30 p.m. Friday, then take on No. 20 Washington at noon Sunday.

Friday’s match historically favors Penn State. The last time the two teams met was last season, when the blue and white defeated the Wildcats 3-1. The Nittany Lions have won the last 13 matches.

Penn State is coming off a big win against Iowa’s Hawkeyes, after a heavy loss against rival and top-ranked Nebraska. In her game against the Hawkeyes, Kennedy Martin contributed 24 total kills, acting as an offensive anchor all match.

The Nittany Lions struggled to come back after a point deficit in the first set; however, the subsequent three showcased relentless offensive talent. Along with Martin, Haley Burgdorf and Whitney Lauenstein combined for 24 kills, making it difficult for Iowa to score. Regardless of one-point trades, Penn State remained in the lead for a majority of the latter three sets.

The Martin-Launstein duo also led in Penn State’s recent loss to Nebraska, despite being swept. Martin totaled 17 kills while Launstein contributed 12.

Lauenstein was able to come up big in tough moments for the Nittany Lions, especially when comebacks seemed promising in the first and second sets. The outside hitter also contributed three blocks.

Going into Friday’s match, a front line featuring Martin and Launstein, paired with setter Alexis Stucky, will pose a strong front and make it difficult for the Wildcats to find holes in Penn State’s defense.

Northwestern is 7-8 overall on the season and played its first conference match Sept. 24. The Wildcats have yet to win against a conference opponent, being swept by UCLA and Minnesota, and losing 3-1 against Ohio State.

On the contrary, Washington poses more of a threat towards Penn State. The last time the blue and white saw the Huskies, it lost in a tight match, 3-2. Washington is currently 12-1 overall, with three conference wins. Along with their conference success, the Huskies are 3-0 on the road.

History is only slightly on Penn State’s side, as it holds a 4-3 advantage in the all-time series history.

The Huskies are coming off a 3-0 win against then-No.10 Purdue; however, they still have a match against Ohio State on Friday, before they take on the Nittany Lions.

In Washington’s match against Purdue, Simona Mateska and Kylie Kleckner each totaled 11 kills. Mateska had a double-double after she also contributed 13 digs. Kleckner halved that amount, adding eight digs of her own.

In her first season with the Huskies, sophomore outside hitter Mateska earned AVCA All-North Region honorable mention, and shows promise in creating obstacles for Martin as she already has 18 blocks and 137 digs in the 2026 season.

Sunday’s match will be a true test for Penn State. It can be beneficial for a team to experience an early-season conference loss; however, these games can set the tone for the rest of conference play.

Martin, Lauenstein and Stucky’s offensive line will give Penn State a good foundation and should be a competitive matchup for Washington.

title: Players to watch | QB Jayden Maiva, WR Kayden Dixon-Wyatt lead USC’s high-powered offense
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will host the most talented team it’s faced thus far in the White Out with No. 19 USC heading to Happy Valley.

The Trojans are 5-1 on the season, with their only loss coming to Oregon, 41-27. The high-octane offense under Lincoln Riley ranks No. 12 in the country in passing, averaging 311.7 yards per game. However, multiple freshmen receiving threats are questionable to play, including tight end Mark Bowman and wide receiver Trent Moseley.

Here’s some USC players to watch ahead of Saturday’s game.

Jayden Maiava, quarterback

Jayden Maiava is the centerpiece of USC’s offense. The senior quarterback has thrown for at least 245 yards in all six of the Trojans’ games this season, but he’ll now face a defense that has allowed 119.6 yards per game in the air.

Against Oregon, Maiava threw for 326 yards and two touchdowns. However, he hasn’t posed much of a threat in the run game, rushing 18 times for -4 yards. The sacks haven’t factored into that too much, as he’s only gone down five times this year.

Maiava has a 68.6% completion percentage on the season, but his efficiency has dropped since Big Ten play has started with a 59.3% completion percentage in his three Big Ten games.

Kayden Dixon-Wyatt, wide receiver

The Trojans’ top receiver in the first half of the season, Kayden Dixon-Wyatt has given defenses fits so far.

Dixon-Wyatt is one of multiple breakout freshmen in Riley’s top-ranked 2026 recruiting class. Despite leading the team in receiving, he wasn’t featured in USC’s close victory over Washington.

In five games, the freshman has totaled 25 catches for 372 yards and three touchdowns. He had a touchdown reception called back against Washington that kept him off the stat sheet.

It’s not surprising that USC’s lowest scoring effort came when Dixon-Wyatt didn’t tally a catch, and if Penn State wants to limit the Trojans’ offense, the likes of cornerbacks Daryus Dixson and Audavion Collins will have to shut down Dixon-Wyatt like Washington did.

Deven Bryant, linebacker

Linebacker Deven Bryant is one of USC’s leaders on the defensive side. Bryant transferred from Washington this past offseason after three seasons with the Huskies. In his first year at USC, he’s second on the team in tackles with 33.

Bryant is the Trojans’ run-stopping linebacker, oftentimes reading the play and making a stop at the line of scrimmage. Against Rutgers, Bryant notched eight tackles and was a big part in limiting Rutgers running back Antwan Raymond to 5.8 yards per carry.

This will be Bryant’s second White Out at Beaver Stadium, as he played for Washington in 2024 when the Huskies traveled across the country. Bryant notched one tackle in their loss to Penn State, his only tackle of the season.

Bryant will be one of the players to watch when limiting Penn State’s rushing attack. The run hasn’t produced much outside of the Nittany Lions’ win over Buffalo, so the linebacker’s run stuffing ability could be a big reason Penn State’s run game continues to remain stagnant.

Prophet Brown, safety

In the back end, safety Prophet Brown has made an impact in all facets of the game defensively.

The senior has two interceptions, including one he returned 99 yards for a pick six against Rutgers. His touchdown allowed USC to pull ahead by two scores in a game that was a lot closer than the Trojans wanted.

Brown has been given the ability to roam in the secondary, which has allowed him to make plays on potential deep shots. His two passes broken up are tied for the team lead in an otherwise struggling secondary.

Penn State has shown it wants to push the ball down the field, and while it hasn’t been too successful since Koby Howard’s injury, it could spark at any moment. Brown’s freedom to fly around in the back end could continue to limit any chance of the Nittany Lions’ big play ability on Saturday.

title: Penn State vs. USC preview | Betting odds, matchup info, more ahead of White Out
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
One of the most anticipated moments of the year for Penn State is nearly here as it welcomes USC to Beaver Stadium for the White Out game on Saturday, which is slated to kick off at 7:30 p.m.

The Trojans hold a one-game lead in the all-time series, having won six of the 11 matchups between the two. However, the Nittany Lions have a chance to even things up this weekend.

Here’s more information on the weather, betting odds and what to look for from both teams during the Week 6 matchup.

Forecast

Fall is finally here, and the weather will reflect that Saturday night with a clear, but cool, forecast.

According to AccuWeather, the temperature during the evening will be 53 degrees with small wind gusts of 7 mph.

There’s a 25% probability of precipitation, but no expected rainfall.

Betting, how to watch

While USC is ranked No. 19 in the AP Poll and Penn State is unranked, the Nittany Lions enter the White Out as 1.5-point favorites, according to FanDuel.

The over/under is set at 54.5 points, meaning a 28-26 Penn State victory is what the sportsbooks are projecting.

The game will be broadcast on NBC or streamed live on Peacock. Tickets are available for as low as $54 on Ticketmaster, much lower than the $250 get-in price for last year’s White Out against Oregon.

About USC

The Trojans come to Happy Valley as the highest-ranked team the Nittany Lions have faced so far. Through five weeks, they’ve won all but one game, losing to Oregon two weeks ago.

USC’s offense has performed among the best in the Big Ten this season, averaging 467.8 yards and 37.3 points per game.

Redshirt senior quarterback Jayden Maiava has led the charge with 15 touchdowns and just three interceptions. However, he’s coming off his worst performance of the season, throwing just one touchdown in a game for the first time this year and giving away an interception for the second straight week.

Maiava’s had a lot of success throwing to a variety of receivers and tight ends, with seven different players having receiving touchdowns. Freshman wide receiver Trent Mosley leads the way with four scores, while wide receiver Kayden Dixon-Wyatt has the most receiving yards with 372.

USC’s offense may be dominant, but its defense has kept things close in many games, including a seven-point victory over Rutgers and a 16-point win against San José State.

The Trojans have given up an average of 348.8 yards per game, including 230.6 yards in the air and 118.2 on the ground.

About Penn State

The Nittany Lions have played their worst football of the season over the last six quarters, blowing a 17-point lead against Wisconsin and falling 34-13 at Northwestern.

Rocco Becht has thrown his only three interceptions of the season during that stretch with just one passing touchdown in garbage time last week. He’s also had several passes batted down at the line of scrimmage and consistently missed his targets in the passing game.

Meanwhile, Penn State’s run game hasn’t found its lead back despite being five games into the season. It appeared James Peoples would take that role against Northwestern, but Carson Hansen earned more yards despite half as many carries.

Defensively, the Nittany Lions continue to boast one of the best pass defenses in the country, allowing just 119.6 passing yards per game — the third-fewest nationally. The run defense, on the other hand, gave up 413 yards against the Wildcats.

Tony Rojas has been arguably the best defensive player this season, recording 21 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, and a pair of interceptions. He’s also been a massive threat in the pass rush, tallying a team-high three sacks.

The rest of Penn State’s pass rush has been underwhelming, as defensive ends Yvan Kemajou and Caleb Bacon are the only edge rushers with a sack in 2026.

If the Nittany Lions want to snap their two-game losing streak and win their second straight game against USC, all aspects of the offense and defense will have to be back and firing on all cylinders.

title: Dueling column | Who should be Penn State women’s hockey’s starting goaltender?
author: Rafael Rivera & Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s starting goaltender position has been a popular storyline early in the season.

Through four games, Morgan Stickney and Maddy Campbell have split the position. Jeff Kampersal and his coaching staff have used these matches to evaluate their performance in order to determine who’ll take over the role permanently.

While they continue to watch the competition, we’ve given our own verdict on who should become the Nittany Lions starting goaltender.

Gavin Leonard: Maddy Campbell

Although Stickney has already made her mark as an impressive freshman goaltender, Campbell offers more continuity and has the performances to prove she's reliable.

As a sophomore, Campbell has a year of experience under her belt. During the 2025-26 season, Campbell posted a .935 save percentage while notching 187 saves over eight starts, with four of those games resulting in shutouts.

In her freshman year, the Courtice, Ontario, native gave Kampersal and his coaching staff a look at what she could do in a full-time role.

While Campbell played very few games as a backup, she spent the year adjusting to the pace and physicality of collegiate hockey, Kampersal’s expectations, and playing at Pegula Ice Arena.

Campbell also had the opportunity to watch and learn from a two-time AHA Goaltender of the Year award winner in Katie DeSa. Now that she’s accustomed to the various aspects of the job, she is primed for a promotion.

When Campbell has faced elite competition this season, she’s played up to par. In a 2-1 loss to No. 2 Ohio State, Campbell saved 31 shots to support a .939 save percentage.

Performing extremely well against one of the best programs in the nation should provide more evidence as to why Campbell should be the anchor of the Nittany Lions defense.

Both goaltenders have already built strong arguments, which makes the decision especially difficult. Yet the deciding factor is Campbell’s commitment to the program, which suggests she deserves the gig.

Campbell spent her freshman year patiently waiting behind DeSa, and she has yet to explain why she doesn’t deserve full ownership of the crease. Starting Campbell rewards her not only for her performances, but also for her willingness to wait her turn.

Rafael Rivera: Morgan Stickney

Campbell has no doubt been a solid option in the net for the Nittany Lions this past year, getting experience watching and learning from former starting netminder DeSa, but I think that Stickney has the higher ceiling in net.

Stickney came to State College with an eye-popping resume, posting a 1.288 GAA and .950 save percentage with 13 shutouts at Shattuck-St. Mary's last season. The true freshman has also already proved herself on the international stage, as Stickney played for Team USA at the U18 World Championships in 2025 and 2026.

In 2025 she posted a .957 save percentage and .67 GAA while making the tournament All-Star Team. In 2026, she recorded two shutouts and helped Team USA claim a gold medal in a 2-0 victory over Canada in the championship game. Her resume shows that she can handle pressure when Penn State is in a tight game with one of the nation's best.

Stickney has already shown she can handle Penn State's biggest games as she was tested early in the season against No. 2 Ohio State. The season-opening series against the Buckeyes was interesting because both keepers got a chance. Stickney made 44 saves in a 2-1 overtime loss in Game 1 of the series and Campbell made 31 saves in the 2-1 loss in the second game.

Even though the Nittany Lions lost, Stickney’s 44 saves against the No. 2 team in the country in her first collegiate game are more than impressive. The St. Charles, Missouri native also showed that she can respond when Penn State isn't playing its best hockey in front of her.

Against Robert Morris, the Nittany Lions fell behind 2-0, but Stickney settled down and allowed Penn State to complete the comeback. I feel that that’s the kind of composure you want from your No. 1 goalie.

Stickney's style also gives Penn State a chance to develop a true No. 1. Campbell has shown she's a reliable NCAA goalie. But if I'm choosing one goalie to build around, I would bet on Stickney's combination of size, athleticism and experience on the international level. She's 5-foot-8 compared with Campbell at 5-foot-6 and has already spent years playing in high-level environments.

Ultimately, Campbell has shown that she belongs at this level, but Stickney has the higher ceiling and the stronger history of doing well against elite competition. If I'm trying to win a National Championship rather than simply find a competent goalie, I'm giving Stickney the opportunity to take the starting job, because what she can do in front of the net can elevate the blue and white to that level.

title: No. 17 Penn State men’s hockey returns key goaltender, adds 2 in between the pipes
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returned one of the best goaltenders in the NCAA, added a CHL goaltender of the year and solid third-stringer to the roster this offseason, cementing its netminder room as one of the best in the nation.

“There's three of them, but they're a team,” coach Guy Gadowsky said during local media day. “They really are, and how they support each other is extremely important for the team as a whole, and also individual performances. I mean, you got to be. We're really happy. I mean, from a group of three goalies, from a goaltending team perspective, I put them up against anybody in the nation.”

Here’s a preview of that unit, starting with the goaltender who assumed the No. 1 role late last season and ran with it.

Josh Fleming

Penn State enjoyed a steady first year out of Fleming, where he flashed his dominance on several occasions. The Canadian finished his freshman season with a 10-7-2 record, a 2.61 goals-against average, and a .924 save percentage, while saving 15.2 goals above expected.

He earned All-Big Ten honorable mention and was stellar in Penn State’s NCAA Tournament game against Minnesota-Duluth, allowing just two goals on 38 shots, which equated to a .947 save percentage. Overall, he elevated his play in the postseason, saving 63 of 67 shots for a .940 save percentage. Fleming also totaled two shutouts, both in the regular season against LIU and Minnesota.

The sophomore’s glaring strengths are his ability to go post-to-post in an instant and his silky-smooth play behind the net along the boards.

Like last year, he’ll likely split duties with teammate Ryder Fetterolf, but there’s no doubt he’s entering 2026 as the starter and one of the better goaltenders in the country.

“We have a great one (netminder) to begin with,” Gadowsky said. “Josh Fleming has been excellent, and analytically, he's excellent. He's one of the top goalies in the nation. He certainly was last year.”

Ryder Fetterolf

Fetterolf was the CHL goaltender of the year and was selected in the fourth round of the NHL Draft by the Carolina Hurricanes in June. He’s one of, if not the most, highly regarded newcomers on Penn State’s roster.

He sported a 2.07 goals-against average and .923 save percentage in the OHL last season with the Ottawa 67’s, playing in 41 games and steering his team to a 29-9-3 record. Fetterolf is also coming off a dominant two-year run, where he was a force in the OHL and with Gilmour Academy's PPHL 18u and USHS-Prep teams.

He recorded a 1.83 goals-against average and .930 save percentage in the PPHL 18u, while posting a 1.64 goals-against average and .940 save percentage with the USHS-Prep team.

The Pennsylvania native is going to make an impact right away, likely splitting games with Fleming from the jump.

“Fetterolf an NHL draft choice that was OHL goalie of the year, and he's coming in with a lot of expectations. And I love the fact that we have two guys that are really going to battle out,” Gadowsky said. “… He is a competitor. There's different guys that succeed in different ways, and goaltenders are no exception. And some are very technical, etc. This guy is a competitor, and so he fits our locker room so well. He raises the competitiveness of everybody on our team.”

Crew Petty

Petty, also coming from Gilmour Academy, will be the third-string goaltender. Funnily enough, Fetterolf recruited Petty to Penn State, telling Gadowsky that he’s “an awesome guy and a great guy.”

Gadowsky described Petty as a “big athlete,” and he’s going to likely get some burn this year. He’s coming off a 33-game season with the USHS-Prep Gilmour Academy team, where he posted a 2.19 goals-against average and a .919 save percentage.

He finished his 2025-26 campaign with four games in the MPHL, posting a 0.79 goals-against average and a .954 save percentage.

title: Club baseball captures championships, hearts as a quiet Penn State dynasty
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
“We’ve got bats and s—t.” That’s the refrain Greg “Sandy” Sanderson, the eventual founder of the National Club Baseball Association, used to convince students when he and his classmates built the Penn State Baseball Club (PSBC) in the late 1990s.

The club now has six national championships to its name and has made the National Club Baseball Association (NCBA) DI World Series 18 times since 2001. No one’s questioning if Jacob McGuire and AJ Capizzi have bats.

McGuire, the club’s president, and Capizzi, the 2025-26 treasurer, both credited their success to the culture set by past teams.

Once Sanderson and club founder Dan Snyder convinced prospective players that they were more than “guys getting together, watching MLB and swapping baseball cards,” the ascension was quick. The PSCB played its first intercollegiate game when Sanderson got a call from former Montgomery County Community College baseball coach Lou Lombardo.

Lombardo got word from his daughter, then a Penn State student, that a baseball club was in the works in Happy Valley. He reached out to Sanderson and invited the new team to play a two-game series. The Nittany Lions assembled their hand-me-down jerseys with zippers down the front and mismatched hats and split the set 1-1.

“That’s when the lightbulb went off,” Sanderson said. “Imagine if we practiced or prepared and had tryouts and really got the best players available on campus. And that’s when it really took the turn and became more, ‘Let’s go play other schools.’”

That’s exactly what they did. Sanderson began organizing trips to play other schools, including a spring break trip to Panama City, Florida, that the club still takes today.

The first trip down to the Sunshine State was a huge draw. The club rented a Fullington bus and sold extra seats to friends and roommates who wanted to tag along.

“It was 42 seats on the bus; we only needed 30, so we would sell the extra seats to people's roommates that wanted to go on the trip too,” Sanderson said. “There'd be coolers on the bus, and we'd have card games going in the back of the bus. It was just a lot of fun, and everybody was positive, like, ‘we can't wait to get on spring break.’ It was just like a 16-hour bonding ride down there; just how much fun we had on those bus rides is absolutely my number one memory.”

After graduating from Penn State, Sanderson created the NCBA.

“We always felt like Penn State was the best club baseball team we knew about and there was nothing to show for it. There was no national championship, no league to start or to play in,” Sanderson said. “I wrote a letter, printed it out on the computer. In a nutshell, it said, ‘If you have club baseball at your school, call me.’ Dressed up a little nicer than that, but that's the nuts and bolts of it.”

Sanderson quickly became inundated with messages from Colorado State, Texas A&M, Weber State and schools all across the country. Those teams built the foundation of the 34-team inaugural NCBA.

As the league progressed and added more teams, the organization eventually gained enough notoriety that other sports wanted a piece, and CollClubSports was born to help branch out to other club sports. Sanderson’s CollClubSports now includes basketball and flag football for eight total leagues.

In 2007, the NCBA split into two divisions, and Penn State followed suit soon after by adding a Division II team.

Both teams are entirely student-run, and the efforts are spearheaded by the executive board and the coaching staff. The executive board schedules practices, which are held for both teams together at the State College Teener Fields, communicates with university officials and the league and facilitates travel.

They prepare practice plans, run practices and make all of the game decisions a major league manager would make, while also balancing the academic rigor that comes with being a college student.

Coaching for the club is not just a perfunctory role; many are former players who suffered injuries and then pivoted to the dugout. Many Penn State coaches go on to pursue coaching as a career.

Cam Medic, an assistant coach and Director of Baseball Operations at Gardner-Webb, led Penn State to its 2023 national championship and jumped right into coaching after he graduated.

After reaching the World Series in 2009, the Division II team won the club’s first national championship in 2011. The Division I team joined the party just two years later, winning the 2013 national championship in its 10th World Series appearance.

Penn State won DI national championships in 2018 and 2023 and embarked on a historic three-peat.

The Nittany Lions traveled to Alton, Illinois, for the 2023 World Series with the likes of LSU and Virginia Tech, and defeated Wisconsin-Whitewater in the championship. In 2024, Penn State went back to the Land of Lincoln for a World Series highlighted by two showdowns with Grand Canyon.

“It got to the point where we were five innings into the game in the World Series, a huge high-intensity moment, and we had to essentially leave the field,” Capizzi, a Zelienople, Pennsylvania, native, said. “We went back to our hotel for two to three hours, just waiting to hear.”

After a few innings of evenly matched play, the game went into a weather delay, and both teams retreated to their hotels. They beat Grand Canyon, a game that set them up for a “prime position to then reach the championship game.”

“I think that moment sticks out to me because the perseverance our club had,” Capizzi said.

The 2025 World Series also featured a repeat matchup marred by precipitation. In the second game, they lost to Virginia Tech.

“They sent us into the losers bracket in which we had to claw all the way back to get a rematch with them in the finals, which was exactly what we wanted, right?” McGuire, a Gibsonia, Pennsylvania, native, said. “They're the team that sent you out. You want to get them back.”

Just like the Grand Canyon game a year ago, the championship clash was soaked with rain. McGuire said you could see water coming off of their jerseys.

The game went into extra innings tied at six, and in the bottom of the tenth, first baseman Owen Mathes came through with the bases loaded and two outs. McGuire pitched the final 4 2/3 innings. He said every emotion was going through his mind.

“There's nothing as special as everyone's happy being in that dog pile. It was when we stood up and we looked around and there was tears in everybody's eyes. That is a memory that I will hold forever. And it wasn't so much that it was happy tears because we had just won; it was because of the group,” McGuire said.

The common thread throughout the PSCB is the community that comes with it, McGuire said, and that the team is like his family.

Many players think they’re done as an athlete when they graduate high school, but the club offers another avenue for connection and competition.

“After my senior year, I was pretty ready to hang ‘em up,” Capizzi agreed. “I really didn't want to play anymore, but just the second that I played my first fall league game, went through tryouts — I haven't looked back since.”

Earlier this year, former PSCB players came together to purchase a house in Boalsburg dubbed the “PSBC Lodge.” The lodge is an extension of a group chat of “old balls” that Sanderson said is active nearly every day.

“That's how much it meant to those guys. Their career isn't like mine where they're dealing with this every day,” Sanderson said. “But their experience with the Penn State Baseball Club meant enough for them to invest this much money to build this place for us other guys to come back and all hang out together–pretty awesome.”

For Sanderson, McGuire and Capizzi, Penn State club baseball will be a part of their lives forever. Sanderson said it’s been his life since he joined.

“And then it's spinning off into what's become my career, running the National Club Baseball Association. There's not a day goes by, literally not a day of my life goes by, that someone from the Penn State Baseball Club doesn't send me a text message,” Sanderson said.
