title: ‘I absolutely love this place’ | Penn State's Jackson Smith reveals decision to stay, put NHL on hold
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State defenseman Jackson Smith considered signing his NHL entry-level contract this offseason.

The former No. 14 overall selection in the 2025 NHL Draft revealed he discussed with the Columbus Blue Jackets, the franchise that selected him, his agent and his family about his looming decision.

But Smith, who said in the locker room after last year’s season-ending loss to Minnesota-Duluth in the NCAA tournament, “I’ll remember this feeling, and I’m not going to let it happen again,” ultimately returned to Happy Valley for his sophomore season.

“I could have gone there and tried to make the team, and maybe ended up in the AHL,” Smith said during local media day Tuesday. “But I decided I don't need to rush; I'm still a young kid, I'm trying to play in the NHL for 20 years, not play there when I'm 19, and play there for five years … I want to be the best player I can be when I get there. So if that means taking an extra year in college (I’d do it). I love this place, I was incredibly happy and grateful to be coming back here, and hopefully make the next step.”

Smith, Penn State’s first-ever first-round NHL draft pick, was as advertised his freshman season. The star blue liner finished the 2025-26 campaign with Second Team All-Big Ten honors after ranking second among freshman defensemen in points (26) and leading all Big Ten blue liners in goals (11), which broke a single-season program record.

His seven power-play goals also led the nation among defensemen, while setting the school record for blue liners and jumping to second all-time for all positions.

So imagine what that second-year jump would look like for Smith, who said Tuesday he’s gained 10 to 15 pounds since he came to Penn State in 2025.

“Just my full 200-foot game,” Smith said of what he worked on this offseason. “Just kind of being a bit more of a pest out there, a bit harder to play against in the D-zone, but still not take away from my offensive game — just making a simple play when I need to. Sometimes I feel like I can force some harder plays that don't need to be made at times, but I'm still trying not to take away from the offensive side of my play.”

After losing plenty of upperclassmen leaders this offseason, including Aiden Fink, Charlie Cerrato, Matt DiMarsico and Jarod Crespo, Smith thought it was time to take on more of a leadership role. So he had two conversations with coach Guy Gadowsky — one at the end of last year and one in the summer — to discuss how to maintain the team’s culture.

In his talks with his coach, Smith acknowledged the difficulties of CHL players transitioning to college hockey, as he experienced them himself just a year ago. He decided he wanted to help his new teammates transition to the NCAA quickly.

“I can just bring a lot to the table, especially with the new CHL guys; there's a lot of them coming in now, and there will be more next year,” Smith said. “So it's just teaching them how to play college and teaching them how for the next guys that come in.

Gadowsky spoke on the importance of having a former first-round draft pick, someone of Smith’s stature, take on that role is important, as he’s a player his teammates can lean on.

“It's just a process, and I'm still trying to learn, and I still learn off them, and they learn off me,” Smith said. “It's been fun, but just being a bit more of a veteran, especially with not a lot of our junior class being here anymore, I definitely had to make a step and mature a lot.”

Smith described last season as “the best year of my life,” and said on many accounts that Penn State means so much to him. He said it in the locker room after the Nittany Lions’ season flatlined in Albany, and he echoed that Tuesday in the back corner of Pegula Ice Arena’s media room.

“I absolutely love this place,” Smith said. “Everything about this place — it's just like it's college, like it's just all you have here is college, and it's amazing the atmosphere that we bring to this arena and all the sporting events here. It's pretty incredible. Just being able to walk around with the boys and be so close to everybody. Like, every house is super close; everybody lives really close. So just everything about this place has been incredible. Obviously, the staff here and just everybody in Penn State has been amazing to me and our team — I can't be more grateful.”

title: SEE IT: Penn State men's hockey alum Gavin McKenna nets first two NHL points
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a quiet start with the Toronto Maple Leafs, Gavin McKenna has his first two professional points.

The No. 1 overall pick in this year's NHL Draft was credited with an assist on his first professional point after his pass found linemate John Tavares, who took it the length of the ice and finished with a shot off the crossbar. It was reported earlier this summer that the pair actually would live together in Tavares' home through McKenna's debut.

McKenna's first goal came less than 10 minutes later.

After a pass found McKenna open in the right faceoff dot, he fired a blistering shot up and over the shoulder of Nashville Predators goaltender Juuse Saros.

The 18-year-old's big performance came in his fourth career game, as McKenna soon returns to the ice after his big night for a Thursday clash against the Las Vegas Golden Knights.

title: Penn State still searching for identity as midpoint of season approaches
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Entering the biggest game of the season so far, Matt Campbell and the players made it clear Tuesday that the team is still in search of what defines them, especially on the offensive side of the ball.

“The reality of it is, we lack an identity,” Campbell said. “We lack who we want to be and where we need to be. And I think you know all of those things come back a little bit fundamentally.”

Penn State’s struggles the past two weeks on offense come from the lack of success in both aspects of the unit. With Koby Howard healthy, there was more of an identity, with him being the consistent and reliable receiver.

Now, the team is still searching for answers after five weeks, especially on offense, as it’s found difficulties moving the ball and getting into a rhythm.

“We just don't really know if we’re a run team or a pass team right now, and so I think for all of us, we're going back immediately to the drawing board, going back to the meeting rooms, and figuring out what we could do well,” Rocco Becht said.

With the struggles on offense, Becht is focusing on correcting his accuracy while also working to continue growing the run game. Both issues likely won’t be resolved at the same time, but one getting rectified could help the offense move the ball down the field.

The coaching staff wants to fix things quickly, and going back to the drawing board to find it is part of the process.

“We lack our identity right now across the board, offensively, defensively and on special teams to who we want to be and how we want to win football games,” Campbell said. “I think as we figure out that and continue to unveil that, the ability to be able to lean into a rhythm of a game and how you call the game to kind of lean into winning the football game.”

On the practice field, the players are still putting in the work and practicing to the level the coaches are wanting to see.

Offensive lineman Cooper Cousins has decided to avoid dwelling on the past. His approach to “worry about the next practice” immediately after Tuesday’s practice ended is a mentality that could pave the way to Penn State finding that identity.

Cousins’ mindset is to ultimately help the Nittany Lions’ offense get out of the slump it’s currently in. In the last two games, the offense has scored 26 points combined and has had issues getting into a rhythm.

“We've got great coaches,” Campbell said. “We've got great players. I think the reality is our identity, what allows us to find that consistency that we're lacking to help this offense to continue to move itself forward.”

The toughest part of the schedule is now in front of the Nittany Lions. Penn State hosts USC and has to travel to Michigan and Washington in the next four games, and if the team can’t correct things, the losing streak could last for a while.

It’s a quick turnaround to find all the answers for an offense that put up 291 yards against Northwestern. Despite facing the No. 19 team in the country on Saturday, the Trojans’ defense has struggled, which could be favorable for the spiraling offense.

“Let's make darn sure that the identity that we want to be starts to come out,” Campbell said.

title: ‘Get our swagger back’ | Penn State battles with adversity after 2 straight losses
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rocco Becht has lost many football games throughout his career. He had back-to-back losses in 2024 and four straight losses in 2025, and now, he’s fallen short in this year’s first two Big Ten games.

But in the past, Becht has bounced back from these losing stretches, winning the remaining games each season. He’s carrying that same mindset right now.

“For me, it's digging back to that 2024 season,” Becht said Tuesday. “What did I do? What did I change to get out of that slump? And I think for me, it was coming to work every single day with a positive attitude.”

Penn State’s next chance to right the ship is the White Out game against No. 19 USC, which is the fourth-highest ranked Big Ten team. On the other hand, the Nittany Lions are coming off a 34-13 loss to Northwestern and are one of the seven teams with an 0-2 record in conference play.

Over the last six quarters of play, the Nittany Lions have struggled in all aspects. The offense has failed to generate significant yardage, specifically on the ground, the defense gave up 413 rushing yards against Northwestern and even kicker Ryan Barker missed a field goal.

While the team isn’t where it wants to be performance-wise, it’s stayed true to its core philosophies and is attempting to grow each week with a positive mindset.

“I went in there with positive vibes throughout the whole facility, and I think that just brings everybody up,” Becht said. “Whatever I’m doing, that’s what the whole team is going to be doing, and so that’s how I carry myself every single day. I’m just going to continue to do what I do and believe what I believe.”

But Becht isn’t the only one who’s faced adversity before. The Nittany Lions lost six straight games last year before ending the year winning five straight. More than 50 of those players are back on this year’s squad and facing similar adversity.

“(I’ve) definitely learned some things about our team last year and about myself individually,” right guard Cooper Cousins said. “I see the capabilities that this squad has. I see how hard everybody works. I see everybody attacking. This team’s hungry to go out there and compete for the best fans.”

Following last week’s loss to Northwestern, several players talked about how the practices were less physical due to the short week. That may not have been the best option, as they then said the game wasn’t as physical as they hoped with several players missing tackles.

This Tuesday, the players said they had one of the most physical practices in a long time, flushing the loss and moving forward.

“No matter what adversity you’re going through, whatever hard times you’re going through, you can’t have a poor me mentality,” Cousins said. “You have to grab your lunch pail and go back to work.”

While the Nittany Lions are facing their first sustained bout of adversity this year, it hasn’t shocked them. They knew before the season this would happen at some point, but they’re now working to fight through it.

“There’s going to be adversity that happens every season, it’s not going to be a Cinderella story,” Cousins said. “I think Rocco has done a really great job and phenomenal job getting us all together.”

With seven more conference games on the horizon, Becht knows the team needs to gain its confidence back from earlier this season because they have the potential to be great.

“I think we just have to get our swagger back and walk around like we're the best person at that position,” Becht said. “We just got to be able to have fun and bring that swagger back.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says his team 'lacks an identity'
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell took the podium at Beaver Stadium on Tuesday after Penn State’s loss to Northwestern. The Nittany Lions are headed into their first White Out game under Campbell at 7:30 p.m. Saturday.

Campbell discussed the team’s lack of a real identity, offensive struggles across the board and gave an update on wide receiver Koby Howard.

Here’s more of what he said.

Team identity

Campbell expressed his frustration regarding the lack of a team identity. He noted Penn State has gone through difficult times in the past and has managed to come back stronger, and while he has confidence in his players and coaching staff, the team “isn’t where it needs to be.”

“The reality of it is, we lack an identity,” Campbell said. “We lack who we want to be and where we need to be.”

He said the team lacks identity on offense, defense and in special teams while not playing to the standard they set for themselves. To improve the culture, he said facing adversity is crucial, something they’re going through right now.

Campbell said the team wasn’t where it needed to be after the Buffalo game, so he’s not surprised by the void in identity at this point because the program is newly growing into it in the first season under his leadership.

“You're trying to mold the culture together, and it's a growth process,” Campbell said. “We have to be better, and it starts with my leadership of making sure we get better. But I have great belief in the humans that we have, and we're just not there right now.”

Rocco Becht, offensive concerns

Rocco Becht has been inconsistent in Big Ten action with just one passing touchdown and three interceptions the past two contests. Campbell noted how when the offense struggles, it can “put a spotlight” on the quarterback’s mistakes.

Although Campbell said Becht needs to be better, he was quick to defend his quarterback and said the entire offensive unit around him needs to be more consistent.

“We need to be better with the other 10 people around him too,” Campbell said. “We need to be better in our pass protection at times, we certainly need to be better in terms of our run game. So we can get him into a rhythm, so he can play with great consistency. We haven't been able to do that, and obviously that is frustrating.”

Campbell noted how the Big Ten is a physical conference, but downplayed the switch from the Big 12. He’s played against Big Ten opponents during his time at Iowa State, and said the physicality of the conference is not the primary concern at this stage.

“Where we're at is trying to build a culture, schemes and foundations, “ Campbell said. “So I think the easy thing to say is, ‘is it a physical problem? Is it a lack of physicality?’ I think some of that shows up when you're so inconsistent in some of the detailed things it takes to play good football.”

Update on Howard

Campbell said Howard is still “a couple weeks away” from his return to the field despite Howard implying he’d be back against Michigan on Oct. 17 via his Instagram story a few weeks ago.

Not having him has added to the difficulties in the passing game, as Campbell said Howard was the player who executed against opponents’ top defenders, a role Chase Sowell is charged with in Howard’s absence.

“One thing that Koby brought was consistency,” Campbell said. “He was the guy that was consistently executing. Koby was the guy that was creating matchups.”

Campbell alluded to how many other players were dealing with offseason surgeries, which could be affecting their play now, and the team needs to have a next-man-up mentality in the wake of injuries such as Howard’s. He said this applies across the board, not limited to the wide receiver room.

“There is a little bit of a process of those guys getting back to where we need them to play with the physicality and the detail we need them to play,” Campbell said. “Those aren't excuses, and that happens in every team in the country. We have to make sure simplicity equals velocity.”

title: Penn State notebook | DC D'Anton Lynn reflects on poor performance from his run defense
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Three days after Penn State’s defense allowed 506 yards to Northwestern, D’Anton Lynn took the podium in Beaver Stadium ahead of the Nittany Lions’ White Out against USC.

Lynn discussed the team’s struggles against the Wildcats on Friday night, the upcoming matchup against his former team and more.

Here’s a look at what he had to say.

Struggles in Evanston

The run game was the most glaring issue in the loss to Northwestern, as Penn State allowed 413 yards on the ground. After watching the film, Lynn said the line of scrimmage was the biggest weakness.

“I don’t know if we won the line of scrimmage once,” Lynn said. “We didn't lose every time, but we didn't win at all.”

As the run defense struggled, Penn State gave up multiple runs of over 30 yards. Several of those came as the result of missed tackles.

Despite those misses, Lynn expressed his confidence in his defense and his linebackers, saying “everyone has done a lot of good things.”

“I would just say the biggest thing is just consistency,” Lynn said. “Consistency in our fits and tackling.”

While the Nittany Lions couldn’t come back and find an answer against the Wildcats, Lynn focused on what it takes to move forward and build success.

“If we have to move guys around, we have to get the different looks,” Lynn said. “We have to put guys in different spots, getting different looks, but put those guys in position to win.”

USC reunion

Lynn spent the 2024-25 seasons at USC before coming to Happy Valley, where he coached against starting quarterback Jayden Maiava during practice.

With the Trojans coming to Beaver Stadium on Saturday, Lynn has experience against Maiava and what he presents offensively. However, coach Lincoln Riley’s playstyle has its difficulties as well.

“He doesn’t have a playbook, he just has plays, and he’s gonna do what his guys do best,” Lynn said. “There's times where he'll present things, and it's like, man, you just don't have an answer for us. You have to keep them guessing.”

The Trojans are coming off a close victory against Washington and are the first top-25 team the Nittany Lions will face this year. Playing against one of the top programs in the Big Ten, Lynn prioritized going back to some of the basics to compete against USC.

“We need to be great on third down,” Lynn said. “We need to be great in the red zone, and we need to stop the run and then don't give them chunk plays.”

Coaching location

Through the first four games of the season, Lynn coached from the booth — a decision that faced a lot of contemplation during fall camp. Against the Wildcats, Lynn started the game in the booth, but moved onto the sidelines after halftime.

“It was just hard to watch from up top,” Lynn said. “Just not being down there with the guys and being able to talk to them, look them in the eye. You don't know what's going on down there, so it just felt better being down there while all that was going on.”

While he made that switch in the second half of Friday’s game, he hasn’t made a decision yet on this weekend’s location, but recognized the benefits of being on the field.

“I just felt better being down there, just making sure, regardless of what the circumstances are, regardless of what's going on on defense, regardless of what's going on on offense,” Lynn said. “When we go out there we have to have the same mentality.”

title: Penn State professors examine concerns about AI's rapid development
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has grown by leaps since ChatGPT’s 2022 launch, leading to concerns that its development is beginning to outpace people’s ability to control it.

These concerns are often exemplified by incidents where AI models break out of their test environments and hack parts of the internet after gaining access to it. This was the case in July, when OpenAI’s models escaped containment during a security test and managed to hack into the AI startup Hugging Face.

This incident has been followed by a series of other hacks by AI models, including successful and unsuccessful breaches into government websites belonging to Canada, Australia and the United States. The Federal Trade Commission has since launched an investigation into the matter.

In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier,” focused on the Hugging Face hack and its ramifications for global AI development. He presented a plan in the essay to slow its progress both in the U.S. and potentially throughout the world.

He wrote that actions need to be taken to verify safety practices and report incidents within AI companies, including embedding evaluators with “employee-like access.” And he wrote about the need to limit AI’s ability to create the next generation of itself in a phenomenon called recursive self-improvement.

Alan Wagner, an aerospace engineering associate professor whose research and interests include AI and machine learning, said he had heard “bits and pieces” of some of the ideas presented in Amodei’s essay. Amodei’s position as Anthropic’s CEO, Wagner said, also makes him well-suited to speak on concerns within the industry.

Wagner is skeptical about whether some of the actions Amodei presented warrant a complete pause at all. He also said he was not convinced a pause of American AI development will cause other countries, like China, to follow suit, out of fear they will be outcompeted in the race for more powerful AI models.

“There's no way, really, to pause AI research globally. And it sort of leaves us in a situation where these things are gonna advance until something bad does happen because of both national competition and international competition,” Wagner said.

Wagner said he is also concerned having evaluators be treated as employees within the companies they are meant to keep in check will cause them to eventually work to protect a company’s interests with AI development over ensuring it is being done safely and in compliance with established policies.

He also said he viewed Amodei’s description of the threats posed by recursive self-improvement in his essay as being too vague and expressed a desire to learn more about why Amodei focused on this aspect of the dangers of rogue AI.

“Presumably, the development of super intelligent AI is not just a matter of having the agent write code: it’s algorithmic development; it's mathematical advances; possibly, it's just scaling, but recursive self-improvement is really not going to improve those things,” Wagner said. “An agent's not gonna go to the Library of Congress and copy books physically, so I'm not sure that these agents are going to be able to scale or improve.”

Wagner also said he predicts AI companies will form an agreement among them to set the terms of a development pause before one ever takes place.

Such negotiations between American AI companies may be possible as Sam Altman and Elon Musk, the CEOs of OpenAI and SpaceX respectively, have been reported to have joined Amodei in calling for a “coordinated slowdown” of artificial intelligence development.

Brian Lennon, a professor of English and comparative literature who specializes in topics related to AI, said he found it hard for him to determine whether Altman and Musk’s statements are completely genuine, given the investments both have made into artificial intelligence infrastructure, such as data centers.

He also said some may interpret Altman and Musk’s comments more cynically by believing they are attempting to convince the U.S. government to enact regulations that would allow their companies to dominate the AI industry by putting them in a position where they are considered “too big to fail.”

Amodei’s own calls for the pacing of AI development also come at a time when Anthropic is expected to go public sometime in November, with investors expecting the company to be valued at between $1.8 to $2 trillion.

“I don't take the entirely cynical position that this is all purely self interest. THAT’S likely to be a strong ingredient of anything involving as much wealth as this industry right now,” Lennon, 55, of State College, Pa. said. “Whatever you think of (Altman and Musk) as people, they're both in charge of an intellectually very challenging situation, so you have to assume that there's some good faith in there somewhere as well.”

Though government action will be required for regulating the long-term development of artificial intelligence, he said, he’s unsure whether this will be enacted under the Trump administration, since its policy on the matter so far has been inconsistent.

Several members of Congress have joined with tech leaders in calling for enacting AI regulations. President Donald Trump has remained resistant to these demands and said all that’s needed to regulate AI development is a “strong and smart president.”

This statement stands in contrast to Trump’s Saturday appointment of National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to become the administration’s “AI Czar;” he’ll develop regulations and safety standards for AI development.

Lennon also pointed to the declaration of Anthropic as a supply chain risk following the collapse of a 2025 contract with the Department of Defense for use of the company’s AI models as another instance when the Trump administration was unusually hands-on in regulating the industry.

Patrick Plaisance, the Don W. Davis professor in ethics for the Donald P. Bellisario College of Communications, said concerns of human control over AI do deserve attention, but they shouldn’t distract from issues stemming from the social, mental and cognitive health impacts of prolonged chatbot usage — which Plaisance has spent some time researching.

Plaisance said AI’s impact on peoples' health, especially socially and mentally, mirrors those seen with the extended use of social media, another industry which received little government regulation in its early stages.

He said the only way to prevent this from happening again with artificial intelligence is through the pressuring of AI companies to enact guardrails. This could be a similar path to what led Meta agree to pay a $17 billion settlement and implement stronger child safety features on Instagram and Facebook after a federal lawsuit filed for these platforms’ addictive effects on children, Plaisance added.

“The single metric of success for chatbots really comes down to engagement. That's all the companies care about, is keeping your eyeballs there,” Plaisance said. “That was the same thing that we allowed to be the metric of success for social media platforms, and we now know the harms that stem from that kind of mindset. It took us 15 to 20 years, and I hope it doesn't take us another 15 or 20 years to realize that we have to grapple with these similar moral questions with AI assistants.”

title: 23 cases of sexual misconduct have been reported to university police since Aug. 19. Penn State has sent no Timely Warnings
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Content warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

Since Aug. 19, 23 cases of sexual misconduct have been reported to University Police and Public Safety (UPPS), according to its Daily Crime Log. These reports include incidents of sexual assault and harassment listed under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA).

These reports occurred during the “Red Zone,” a period from the start of the fall semester to Thanksgiving break where more than 50% of sexual assaults are reported on college campuses.

In the past, Penn State has issued Timely Warnings to alert the community of certain crimes reported to UPPS, especially for cases involving sexual misconduct and sexual assault.

However, the university has not issued a Timely Warning for University Park since Feb. 19, 2025, which was for two separate hazing incidents at both on and off-campus student organizations.

The last Timely Warning for a sexual offense was Nov. 19, 2024.

In 2024, 10 Timely Warnings were sent, eight of which were sexual offenses.

In 2023, 11 Timely warnings were sent, six of which were for sexual offenses and one for stalking under the VAWA.

In 2022, 15 Timely Warnings were sent, 13 of which were for sexual offenses and one for stalking under the VAWA.

Cases of sexual misconduct reported to UPPS in fall 2026

Aug. 19

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall on Aug. 7 in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is not cleared.

Aug. 24

A student reported being harassed at an on-campus property. The case is not cleared.

Aug. 29

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is open.

Sept. 4

A student reported being harassed between Sept. 5 and 6 at an on-campus property. The case is open.

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by an unknown person in a residence hall on Sept. 5 in Porter Hall. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 11

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person at a parking lot outside Beaver Stadium between Aug. 30 and Sept. 11. The case is open.

A student reported being harassed between Aug. 21 and Sept. 11 in Nittany Apartments. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 14

A student reported being harassed at the Intramural Building. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 22

A student reported being harassed between Aug. 24 and Sept. 22 in Pollock Hall. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 23

Sept. 24

Sept. 27

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall on Sept. 25 in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is open.

A student reported being harassed on Sept. 25 in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is open.

Sept. 28

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall between Sept. 24 and 25 in West Halls Residence Complex. The case is not cleared.

A student reported being harassed between Aug. 17 and Sept. 26 on campus. The case is open.

Campus police assisted an outside agency with a reported sexual assault at an off-campus apartment between Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 on West College Avenue. The case is closed.

Oct. 2

A student reported being physically assaulted by a known person on campus between Sept. 21 and 26. The case is not cleared.

Oct. 3

A visitor reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in an unknown location between Oct. 2 and 3. The case is not cleared.

What are Timely Warnings?

In Penn State’s annual security and fire safety report published on Sept. 30, the university described the purpose of Timely Warnings as “an effort to provide timely notice to the campus community in the event of a Clery Act Crime that may pose an ongoing threat.”

UPPS may distribute these warnings through emails, posters, web postings and media, and it has the discretion to determine whether a Timely Warning is required, according to the report. UPPS may issue Timely Warnings for events occurring off campus if the location is frequented by the university population.

The definition says they may issue a Timely Warning for the following crimes: criminal homicide, aggravated assault, sexual assault, burglary, robbery, motor vehicle theft, arson, certain hate crimes, dating violence, dometic violence, stalking and hazing.

The warnings are issued on a “case-by-case basis” based on the following criteria: One of the above listed crimes are reported; the perpetrator has not been apprehended; continuing threat risk

to the safety of other members of the campus community because of this crime; and possible risk of compromising law enforcement effort.

Timely warnings are required by the Jeanne Clery Campus Safety Act, a federal statute governing how colleges and universities that receive federal funding report crimes on and near campus. After a Clery Act crime occurs, campus officials are required to “evaluate if there is a serious or ongoing threat to the campus community,” according to the Clery Center.

In an email to The Daily Collegian, UPPS Public Information Officer Jacqueline Sheader wrote that all reports to UPPS are individually evaluated to determine if they meet Timely Warning criteria.

“Factors that may support a decision not to issue a Timely Warning include situations where the suspect has been identified and apprehended or law enforcement has determined that there is no ongoing danger. University Police also assess the nature of the crime, the circumstances surrounding the incident, the likelihood of recurrence, and the amount of information available to provide a meaningful warning,” Sheader wrote.

Resources

Medical services include Mount Nittany Medical Center; Penn Highlands State College; and University Health Services.

On-campus resources include Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS); the Office of Sexual Misconduct Reporting & Response; the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention, and Community Education (R-VOICE) Center; and The Center for Sexual and Gender Diversity (CSGD).

Off-campus resources include Centre Safe.

title: A look at No. 17 Penn State men’s hockey’s new defensive core
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 17 Penn State will have a new look to its defensive core as it opens the season against No. 15 UConn on Friday.

After losing sophomore Cade Christenson to the transfer portal and both Jarod Crespo and Carter Schade to graduation, the Nittany Lions have a new blueline group debuting this weekend.

Between new additions and key returners, here’s a preview of the blue and white’s 2026-27 defenders.

New Additions

One of Penn State’s biggest offseason additions was former Vermont defender Caeden Herrington. The 6-foot-2 sophomore is a skilled two-way defenseman with offensive upside that has the potential to drive production for the Nittany Lions.

The Los Angeles Kings selected Herrington in the fourth round of the 2025 NHL draft, and he played in 34 games at Vermont, tallying one goal and seven assists. Previously, Herrington skated with the Lincoln Stars of the USHL, serving as an alternate captain and recording 16 goals, the second most in a single season by a Lincoln defenseman.

Another transfer portal addition was former Miami University blueliner, Charlie Michaud.

Michaud brought depth to the RedHawks, appearing in six games before finishing out the 2025-26 season with the Penticton Vees of the WHL. In 35 games, the Denver native tallied 15 assists.

Freshman Ethan Weber is the only Penn State defender new to NCAA play this year. Weber is coming off a productive season in the WHL, playing alongside Michaud with the Vees, where he put up 51 points in 68 games and led the team in scoring among defensemen.

The 6-foot-1 Manhattan Beach, California, native has the potential to add more scoring to Penn State’s blueliners as he develops alongside NCAA veterans.

Key Returners

Sophomore Jackson Smith has built a solid case for one of the best defenders in the Big Ten.

The Calgary, Alberta, native wrapped up his freshman season with an impressive resume — breaking two program records for the most single-season goals by a defenseman (11) and most power-play goals by a defenseman (7), as well as being named to the All-Big Ten Second Team and All-Freshman Team.

Smith, the No. 14 overall pick in the 2025 NHL Draft by the Columbus Blue Jackets, is poised for another big season after being named to the Preseason All-Big Ten Second Team.

Senior Mac Gadowsky is another key returner to Penn State’s defense. Gadowsky, son of Penn State coach Guy Gadowsky, transferred from Army last season.

After leading all defensemen in the country in points and goals during the 2024-25 season and becoming the Black Knights’ first-ever Hobey Baker Award Top-10 Finalist, Gadowsky fell significantly short of his previous offensive production this past season, waiting until the Big Ten Tournament to score his first, and only, goal with the program so far.

Despite the State College, Pennsylvania, native’s pure scoring struggles, he managed 17 assists and finished second for the defensemen on the team in both scoring and blocked shots, with 42.

Both Casey Aman and Nolan Collins are also solid returners for the Nittany Lions.

Aman, entering his senior season, has the ability to slot in almost anywhere in the lineup, used in a range of defensive pairs, as the extra skater, and sometimes even as a forward last season while the blue and white battled an extensive injury bug.

Collins begins his sophomore season after spending most of last year alongside Christenson, and while not the flashiest of scorers, he can generate creative offensive plays while using his 6-foot-4 frame to take a more physical edge.

To round out the defensive group, Nick Fascia’s return will add more depth to the blue and white’s roster.

The sophomore appeared in 25 games last year, registering a goal and three assists before suffering a season-ending injury in February.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | Joey Porter Jr. debuts, Chop Robinson records 1st sack of season
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Week 4 of the NFL season has come and gone, and former Penn Staters were involved all weekend.

The tight ends were once again heavily featured, while a former Penn State cornerback made his season debut with his new team following a mid-week trade.

Here’s what former Nittany Lions stood out on the first weekend of October.

Battle of cats

The Cincinnati Bengals and the Jacksonville Jaguars met in Cincinnati for a matchup that featured four former Penn State offensive players.

Tight end Brenton Strange led the Jaguars in receiving with seven catches for 95 yards, including a failed attempt at a hurdle in which he fumbled, but the ball went out of bounds and no damage was done.

The Jaguars’ leading receiver on the season, Parker Washington, was relatively quiet in Sunday’s game. Washington had one catch for seven yards and a rush for three yards, but he still leads the team with 228 receiving yards on the season. Strange and Washington are the top two receivers on the 3-1 Jaguars.

On the other side, Mike Gesicki found himself in the end zone for the third time this season. In games this season where he’s caught a pass, the former Penn Stater has also scored a touchdown, proving to be a reliable red zone target for Joe Burrow.

The Bengals signed Mitchall Tinsley off the Houston Texans’ practice squad on Sept. 29, and he made his season debut on Sunday. Tinsley caught three passes for 49 yards, including a 29-yard reception down the sideline to push the Bengals into Jaguars’ territory.

With some uncertainty at the position due to injuries to star wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, Tinsley could be a reliable and familiar target for Burrow.

Joey Porter Jr., cornerback, Dallas Cowboys

Former Penn State cornerback Joey Porter Jr. made his Dallas Cowboys debut after being traded from the Pittsburgh Steelers following lengthy contract disputes.

Porter proved once again he’s one of the league’s premier cornerbacks against the Houston Texans.

In the game, Porter played 24 snaps and was targeted just one time on his primary receiver. He has already shown to be a big boost to what was a struggling Cowboys’ defense.

Vega Ioane, offensive lineman, Baltimore Ravens

For the Ravens, Vega Ioane shifted from guard to center after they put both centers on injured reserve.

The move didn’t make a difference for Ioane, who proved to be a dominant force in the run game and pass protection against the Titans. In one rep, he took on defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons one-on-one, neutralizing one of the league’s top defensive tackles.

In just four games, Ioane has already proven to be a valuable pick at No. 14 for the Ravens, showcasing his dominance like he did at Penn State, but also having the versatility to switch positions when the Ravens needed a center.

Firsts of the season

A former Penn State tight end reached the end zone for the first time on Sunday, with New York Giants’ Theo Johnson scoring on his only catch of the game.

Johnson made the catch through a defender to record his second grab of the season. After being the starter last season at tight end, Johnson has taken a step back with the addition of Isaiah Likely. However, he still has played a good amount this season with the Giants using a lot of 12-personnel on offense.

On the defensive side of the ball, former Penn State edge rusher Chop Robinson recorded his first sack of the season against the Minnesota Vikings. Robinson’s presence on the edge was felt all game, tallying eight pressures, three quarterback hits and a 32.3% pressure rate against the Vikings.

His first sack of 2026 was a pure bull rush, pushing the right tackle right into Kyler Murray to end the Vikings’ drive.
